div.head: FREE CHURCHES:
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES:
GIPSY SMITH'S AUTOBIOGRAItY.

"Gipsy Smith: His Life and Work. By Himself"; to be published during the first week of December, by the National Free Church Council, whose missioner Mr. Smith has been for the last four years. In a note this readers the famous evangelist acknowledges the invalu- able literary help which he has received from his friend, Mr. W. Grinton Berry, M.A. Dr. Alexander McLaren, of Manchester, contributes a most interesting introduction to the volume. The distinguished Baptist minister, who has known Gipsy Smith for a long time, says that "that knowledge has discovered to me a character of rare sweetness, goodness, simplicity, and godliness, and pos- sessed of something of that strange attractive- ness with which popular beliefs have endowed his race. But the fascination is explicable on better grounds than magic spells, it is the charm of a nature which draws others to itself, because it goes out to meet them, and is loved because it loves."

div.head: SOME OF THE CONTENTS.
div.p: SOME OF THE CONTENTS.

A writer in the December Free: Church Chronicle, who has been favoured \ with a perusal of the proof sheets, describes his im- pressions of the volume in an interesting article. He says that in an informal way the book is a great work of Christian evi- dences. Gipsy Smith never attempts in his sermons to deal with sceptics. That is not the work for which God has furnished him. But the convincing proofs contained in his book of the truth and unmistakeable reality of con- version make it a very valuable auxiliary of faith. There is, perhaps, no more remarkable episode in personal religious history than the conversion of Cornelius Smith, the evangelist's father. The writer of the article in the Free Church Chronicle declares that God as really and as literally came to Cornelius Smith in his tent as in the Scripture narrative he came to Abra- ham centuries ago in the Arabian desert. The contention is certainly bold, but the writer explains and defends it persuasively. The whole _ article is well worth ettention.

div.head: ROMANTIC LIFE.
div.p: A ROMANTIC LIFE.

The obvious temptation of an evangelist, when he is writing his autobiography, is to fill the book with narratives of remarkable conver- sions. it is only right that such records should have a prominent place, ;but we understand that in Gipsy Smith's book they have not been allowed to overcrowd the volume. The evan- gelist's life has been full of incident and -romance, and in his autobiography he tells his story in simple and graphic language, with great wealth of picturesque detail. The book which is to be published at six shillings, runs to about three hundred and eighty pages, including seventeen illustrations on fine art paper. We -expect that it will be the most successful volume of the present publishing season, and that its popularity will continue and even in- crease as the Gipsy pursdes his life's work. IS IT WORTH WHILE GoING TO CHURCH?

Dr. Horton has written for the National Free Church Council a pamphlet on this press- ing and ever timely subject. It is a very striking production indeed. The writer dreams a dream of a city where there are no churches, no ministers, no Bibles, no Christ, no God. The living bury the dead and wait, drinking, carous- ing, betting, laughing, shouting, until their own time comes. The result is ruin, despair, torment, awl nobs:ody.doulats- that. these arG
thG

-doom , the eternal doom of men. Then the dreamer awakes, hears a bell ring, and seeing people crowding into a little church, follows them. He asks a working man in the congregation if it is worth while to go to Church. He replies: "To worship is to work, and to work is to worship. Christ, the Carpenter of Nazareth, taught me this; and I met Him here." Dr. Horton never imitates anybody, but the style of the sweet 'little pamphlet suggests Mr. Coulson Kernahan.

div.head: MR. MEYER'S FINAL DECISION.
div.p: MR. MEYER'S FINAL DECISION.

The friends of the Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., are not at all surprised to learn that he adheres to his resignation of `his pastorate at Christ Vhurch,Westminster-bridge-road. The publicans and the brothel-keepers of South London have been openly rejoicing in the approach- ing departure of Mr. Meyer from their midst. It is this circumstance alone which has led him to think of cancelling his resignation. Mr. Meyer has complete faith in the future of Christ Church. The resignation does not take effect until next September. He will then be absent from London for four months on visits to Sweden, Germany, and Jamaica. If the church is still pastorless, Mr. Meyer will readily resume his active ministry for the opening months of 1903. Immediately after this he commences his work of conducting missions all over the country.

div.head: AN ANGLICAN ERROR..
div.p: AN ANGLICAN ERROR..

The Rev. Thomas Moore, M.A,, contributes an article to the Church Monthly, on "A New Force for Disestablishment," in which he says that the supreme aim of the National Free Church Council is Disestablishment. That is a grave inaccuracy. The last report presented by the Rev. Thomas Law to the National Coun- cil at Cardiff, in March, consists of over 132 large pages, dealing with a great variety of work, yet we have not been able to discover a single paragraph about Disestablishment! The supreme aim of the National Council is re- ligious and specially evangelistic. It is true, of course, that the National Council does believe in the liberation of the Church from the State. But this is an utterly subordinate item in its programme. There are other serious inaccu- racies in the same article.

div.head: HOW GIRLS ARE LOST TO THE CHURCHES.
div.p: HOW GIRLS ARE LOST TO THE CHURCHES.

Miss Marianne Farningham; who is addressing meetings all over the country in support of the iiew Free Church Girls' Guild, tells a touch- ing story in the Christian World, showing clearly the need for the new Society. A girl was awakened to seriousness by a minister, but left the town before joining the Church, and was lost sight of, not having had her name enrolled in any Church book. • She went to London to seek a situation, and she was dis- appointed day after day. She lived alone in a lodging, she had not a friend in London, and was too brave to let the home people know of her failure. At last, in order to get a little warmth and rest, she one day entered the National Gallery, and there made an acquaintance that ended in her ruin. If the new movement had been established, the Secretary of the Guild in the town where the poor girl lived, would have communicated with the Secretary of a London Guild, and the lonely girl would have been received by kind, good friends, who would have shielded her from the awful peril by which she was overtaken. Miss Farningham hopes that before many years have passed there may be Guild Houses for girls as there are Rowton Houses for Emu.

DUR The evening gowns of the present fashions are mote lovely than they have ever been. There is a disposition to use very rich substantial satins, in cream, silver, or rose tints, cut en princesse, with little adornment save a bertha of rare old lace round the corsage, and a draped flounce round the -bottom of the skirt, looped up with rococo jewel- lery. This style is most becoming to the stately women, for there are some types of beauty which are at a disadvantage in flimsy chiffons and mous- salines. Trains are cut very long, but they spread out in a rounded shape when on the floor, a shape acquired by the skilful cutting of many gores. Hats are not so widely different from what they were 12 months ago. Flatness in shape and out- line has long been prefigured. Wisdom is, indeed, justified in those who buy with an eye to the future, and reject all modes which stamp them- selves as but a fancy of the passing hour.

Corduroy is material which is, being much utilised this season, and it looks especially well in mouse-brown and smoke-grey shades. A smart costume was in deep ivory corduroy (for white is the chic wear this winter, irrespective of ideas of -economy), trimmed with an open handsome ,pattern in woollen lace, outlined with very narrow tends of sable. The bolero, pouched at the waist over a shaped coftelet belt of embroidery, had a deep cape collar of dark sabie, turned back from a small vest lace medallions and embroidered with sprays of leaves in green silk ; at the foot is jewel embroidery to match that on the bolero corsage, which terminates in tassels of jewels strung to- gether. Bands of lace cross the neck attached to a rucked collar of chiffon, and the tight sleeves open over a double puffing of chiffon at the wrists. •The cloak is of emerald green panne, draped with 'a flounce of lace round the hem, headed by a band of sable, and cascaded with lace down the fronts and round the collar.

All the smartly-art— people seem to wear ove.ry light-colourea blouses under their warm winter coats or capes. White or pale pink or blue -8 at i a with lace and the gleam of diamonds; pink ;or-white or maize Chiffon, v ury mus OlValid frilled, and with a liberal trimming of lace; striped or figured crepe in pale and pretty colours —all these appear to be the very height of the ;fashion. They afford a means of being very orna- mentally dressed at no sacrifice of comfort or con- •venience, for the warmest possible " neathies " •may be donned under the satin or muslin or crape .or fluted gauze. On one day of this week a lady dressed in black cloth and dark furs went into a ipictnre gallery, and, loosening her coat, revealed a 'blue silk muslin blouse strapped across down the 'front with bars of darker blue, a shade of corn- 'flower, each strap held down by twc small paste buttons. The lace bow at the neck was black with a relief of white tulle, the whole held by a .sparkling brooch.

A very soft and rather thick silk composed a charming full-length toilette. The skirt has a tunic of folds overlaid with ochre-tinted lace and a very deep lace flounce; the bodice is ti full bebol one of accordion-pleated chiffon, over which is arranged a folded bolero encrusted with lace at the.edge. A berthe of lace finishes it, held to. gather by a chiffon bow, and chiffon roses, deep damask and blush pink in hue, provide the only touch of real colour in the whole scheme worn upon the decolletage and behind the left ear. Folds more properly express the deep tucks now fashionable than the other more frequently used term, but tucks are seen on the chiffon sash that is the gossamer-like completion of the whole arrange- ments. The re-appearance of the old-fashioned flowered silk waistcoats is not only agreeable as recalling a picturesque period of dross, but also serves -two good ends. One is the revival of the bro- caded materials, and the other the employment of skilled embroidery hands. Some of the bye- Hest designs are seen on these waistcoats, narrow as they are, for the fronts of the coats come far forward upon them. A pearl coloured satin is em- broidered with tiny clusters of the smallest possible violets and heather, both in tones of reddish mauve.

' The newest blouses for home or theatre wear are -of point d'esprit net, in a pale ecru tint, pouched over a deep waist-band, with the new sleeves, and flchu collar, knotted into long ends in front of em- broidered tambour work These are ideal for young girls, being so simple yet withal so dainty. Point d'esprit net is also requisitioned for stock ties, and very fresh and attractive they look, easily washed when soiled. The two most prevalent forms of corsage are the blouse and the bolero. Nine dresses out of 10 are sure to be made in one or other of these styles.
Your loving JENNIE.

div.head: WOMEN'S OHM.
div.p: WOMEN'S OHM.

The new Royal crowns are only new in the sense that they will be remade from old ones. St Edward's crown which is used by the Archbishop of Canterbury for th purpose of crowning the Sovereign, is never altered,bute this only dates from the time of Charles 11, the origina one having been destroyed during the Civil War. The crown now being altered for Queen Alexandra was first worn by the Queen of James 11, and the Imperial State Crown, which will be worn by the King during the greater part of the coronation ceremony, was made for Queen Victoria in 1838. Its most precious gem is the famous ruby, worn by Henry V at Agincourt, and alto- gether it contains over 3,000 jewels,and weighs betwesn two and three pounds. The ,Kol3-i-Noor diamond, which, it is stated, will appear in the new crown being prepared for Queen Alexandra, has long been eclipsed by larger gems. The Emperor of Russia is believed to have the largest diamond in the world, which is known as the Orloff diamond. The Emperor of Austria could probably pro- duce the next largest, and there are several others that would come before the Koh-l-Noor.elThe famous Pitt,or Orleans diamond was considerably larger in its original state, but it was greatly reduced by bad cutting before it became one of the French Crown jewels. These were stolen during the stormy days of the Revolution, but some were afterwards recovered. The Hope diamond which has recently been sold to an American for, it is said, £30,C00 or £35,000, was part of a single stone in the French Regalia, which was stolen whilst in the charge of the Paris Commune. Everyone will be interested in the new coinage, and the new postage stamps, which are to make their appearance with the New Year. The colour of the penny stamp is to be changed to a carmine red, and the likeness of King Edward will look to the left, as we have long been accustomed to, in that of Queen Victoria. On the coinage it is usual for the likeness of the Sovereign to be reversed with each succeeding reign, but in the case of the stamps, this would make King Edward looking away from the letter, or in other words, turning his back on the addressee. It is rather sad news for the little folks that no new bright coinage is to be issued this Christmas time. The Bank of England has, for many years. assisted the public in keeping up the old-established practice of giving Christmas boxes in bright new silver, but this year there will be no such special issue, and there will consequently be some :diffi- culty in persuading the little folks, that the old and worn coin is just as good as the bright new one. For the past year or two, London has suffered from an apparent dearth of boys. No one can explain why it is, hut there is a difficulty in obtaining page-boys, messenger-boys, office-boye, van-boys, and so on, never before experienced. Some people put it down to the war. We know that this had'a most mysterious influence in putting up the prices of household articles, but it never created any unusual demand for boys, and as many fathers were away at the front, one would think that there was a greater need than ever, for the rising generation to begin earning wages. Any how the diffi- culty in obtaining boys, has led to the employment of young girls of fourteen and fifteen, by some of the Telegraph and Messenger Agencies in London. It is not however a desirable innovation, as running the streets is not the best training for young girls, nor does it fit them for other employment when they outgrow such work. The prices realised for some of the more valuable furs, seem to indicate that it will not be long before the sources of supply become extinct. At different times we hear that the seals are rapidly being exterminated, but sealfkin, which is not perhaps, quite so much worn this winter, is 3till moderate in price as compared with other furs. It is for instance no uncommon thing for the skin of the Russian Sable Marten, to realise as much as £4OO or £5OO, and the fur of the Silver Fox is also mcst expensive. It would seem that it will hot be long before these beautiful and costly furs are beyond the reach of even the most wealthy. Oce is frequently startled to see women taking their walks and drives abroad, in apparently inadequate out- door garments,but the deficiency is usually made up by an under bodice of wash leather, which is exceedingly warm. Care however, should be taken that such a garment is sufficiently ventilated, and if this is not pro- vided for, down the seams, holes should be punched through in different places. These should be not merely pierced, hut an open aperture made by punching out te e material. The fashionable woman's petticoat often costs more than the gown that covers it, the richest of brocade,and the finest of lace being deemed necessary by the very smart for such " creations." Lesser lights, however, who require to think many times before spending as many shillings as fashionable folks do pounds, on a " frillie," can, if possessed of clever fingers, do much for themselves, and obtain considerable variation for their money. One black silk petticoat, the fabric per- chance having done its duty as a skirt, should be run up, care being taken that it fits perfectly about the hips, and that it flows out in the approved fashion about the- feet. Then a shaped silk flounce to match each costume with which it will be worn. should be fashioned,the top being neatly finished on, to fit that portio,...t the to which it is to be applied. Next, buttonholes must be made, at intervals of about three inches, along the top of the flounce, buttons to correspond being fixed upon the skirt. A series of changes are thus possible at little coat. A black lace flounce fixed to the skirt above the buttons, so that it falls over the removable flounce, is a distinct improvement. ' Never surely, were artificial ilewers more beautiful I than they are at the !present time, the colouring is really exquisite, and the mixture of velvet, silk and chiffon, of which the best are composed, give an unusual softness and reality to the blooms. The floral garni- tures sold ready for the shoulders of evening bodices, are lovely indeed, and will be much appreciated by girls whose allowances are limited, and frocks few. An eldefly black gown Can be rendered quite smart and fresh looking, by such an addition, and if carefully worn, the clusters and trails can later on be dissected and employed for trimming summer hats and toques. A note should be made of these garnitures on our list of ' Christmas presents to be searched for. A book from the pen of the authoress of " Little Lord Fauntleroy is very welcome,and Mrs Hodgson Burnett's latest work " The making of a Marehionese "(Smith, Elder and Co.) will in no way disappoint her wide circle of readers. As a poi trait painter, this distinguished authoress is particularly successful, as those of us who are familiar with her several books—among them "That Lass of Lowries " written while still a girl in ter teens, and " A Lady of Quality "—know full well. Christmas Pudding.—Take two pounds each of suet (well chepped) stoned raisins, sultanas (wash3d, picked, and dried), currants (washed, picked and dried), fine breadcrumbs, and brown sugar. Chop finely one pound of candied peel, blanch and chop half a pound of almonds, peel, and chop one pound of apples, mix well, and sift in two ounces of mixed spice, also half a pound of flour. Beat up five eggs, add half a pint of ale, and a glass of rum, and mix thoroughly. Roil in a cloth for six hcurs. _ _ _

div.head: RAILWAY SMASH AT WILDERS-
div.p: RAILWAY SMASH AT WILDERS-
POOL.

prevallod at half-pant . During the drnse fog which seven on Surday morning a collision occurred on the Londe n and Nortt-Western line near Wilderspool Cress- logs. It appears that a goods train was standing stationary near Messrs Fletcher Russell's works, when another goods train on its way from Hull to Liverpool crashed into the rear of it. The force of the impact derailed the brakesrrian's van and four waggons, and the contents of the waggons, consisting of red ochre and lime were bestrewn about the line. One of the waggons was thrown over the embankment and several were badly damaged. The brakeeman cf the stationary train and the driver of the collidirg engine had narrow es- capes. The brakesman was severely shaken and also sustained injuries to his head. He was taken to the Infirmary but after his injuries had been attended to he was allowed to proceed home. Mr depinall, station- master at Bank Quay, and the night stationmaster and other cfficials were soon on the scene, as well as a large breakdown gang, and the resul' was that the line was cleared for traffic at half-past ten.

SOUTH LANCASHIRE VOLUN-
TEERS IN SOUTH AFRICA.* Captain Appleton 's Book.

Captain Appleton has published his book" The Volunteer Service Company (Ist South Lancashire Regiment) in south Africa," and it proves to be a com- plete work of its kind. Every one of its 200 pages bears evidence of the greatest care having been exercised is its compilation, and there is no doubt that it will be a standard work, an official and authoritative contribu- tion to the military history of South Lancashire. The Active Service Company, formed from the 151 and 2nd Volunteer Battalions (Warrington, Earlestown, St Helens, and Widnes) enrolled in January, 1900. They went south as soon as they could be equipped, and they returned in June of the present year, so that they were on active service about eighteen months. How they spent that time is graphically,humorously, sarcastically, good naturedly told in the pages of this book, which is the joint production of the whole Company. Though the Company visited Cape Calony,NataLthe Transvaal and the Orange River Colony, it was their lot to see , very little actual fighing. As I Company of the Ist South Lancashires, whom they joined soon after the battalion had taken a leading part in the final and suc- cessful attack upon the besiegers of Ladymith—their Colonel, Colonel O'Leary, it will be remembered falling in the hour of victory—they were absorbed into the Lancashire Brigade and the Bth of June, just twelve months before the date of their arrival home, saw them under fire for the first time in Botha's Pass, which General Buller won, preparatory to finally clearing Natal of the Boers. The Company were the object of the fire of a porn-porn, but no one was hurt. A farm fight in which a portion of the Company were engaged at Kromdraai, in the Transvaal, completes the tale of the actual fighting experiences of the Company. Fortun- ately, the Company had not a man either killed or wounded, but tbey lost five men through enteric fever or other forms of disease. A great deal of useful work, however, was performed on the lines of communication, on outpost duty and in guarding the Boer prisoners. Among the treks in which the Company bare a part was one of nearly seven weeks' duration during which they covered over 300 miles without having a chance to refit and oftentimes being hard pressed even for food.

However, the men took the sunshine with the clouds and Captain Appleton's book is a faithful reflection of the good sense and cheerfulness they imported into their ofttimes thankless task. As a whole the Company seems to have had the saving grace of humour. Lauce- Corporal W. Ashton' commeat after a night when on the trek, in which tents were not to he had and sleep had to be taken on the ground hardened by frost, is There are several redeeming features about sleeing in the open. You cannot fall out of bed; bepldea, you haven't the trouble of dressing yourself or the anxiety of choosing what to wear.

After the 300 miles trek came rest at Gras Kop, and the Company, thin and ragged, " rapidly and visibly increased in weight," to quote Lieutenant L3WiS7EI com- forting record. If the men were wet through they con- gratulated themselves on the fact that they could not get wett*. When the time came that they were think- ing of coming home, and they had actually been started upon that pleasure-giving journey, but were suddenly sent into the Orange River Colony for a further spell of active service, they recon- ciled themselves with the reflection that the army could nct manage without the South Lancashire Volunteers. But the funniest thing set down to the credit of this very funny company occurs in Lance Corporal Aribton's account of the Botha' s Pass engagement. The pom-pom fire already referred to was followed by a whistling of bullets overhead, for which a man of the Company, a collier, showed his contempt and his ruling passion for a joke by asking his companion : " What's them, Jem, arena' they bride ? " . .

A joke which runs this one a close race, and is al- most as grim, is told by Sergeant P Hooke in his article on" Outpost at Weasel's Nek." A poultry yard had hien raidcd, and, as eggs were a luxury, "of course, good-natured-like, the men made a present of them to Captain Appleton," who accepted the gift in a manner that accorded well with its importance, but he saw the Sergeant some time afterwards, and, in., a " stage whisper," Said to him, sadly but evidently Toost truly : " Sergeant Rooke, those eggs were bad ! " Lance-Corporal S F Moss is a large and most agree- able contributor, who, among other things, gives a fine description of" A visit to Bulwana," in which he tells tut "that it is a bad thing to think and is not included In the duties of a soldier." The same writer's descrip- tion of a sandstorm is brief but picturesque and convincing It is impossible to see more than a few yards. Occasionally one can hear a biscuit tin about two feet long bounding in his direction, being borne along by the force of the wind. Judging by the intervals between the bumps on the ground it sounds as if the tin were doing twenty yards at a leap. It cannot be seen as the duit is so thick, and all a fellow can do is to turn his back to the sound and trust to Providene. A sigh of relief escapes as the noise fades again." We get at firs:-hand many interesting passages on emsjavta that have Gest much controversy at home. Captain Appleton. In hla Diary "—a complete account of the doings of the Company—gives us,in a few words, a whole chapter on the vexed question of farm burning. Under date September 4th he says : Marched off at 6.30 a in., eight miles in direction of Wakkerstroom. Major Adam commanded Advance Guard which blew up a farm from which, while white flag was flying, one scout and a Kaffir guide bad been treacherously shot. Not a pleasant sight to see the family sitting at a safe distance among their furnitur and household goods watching their home go up lute the air, but unfortunately nothing else will satisfy them. and the women are even more treacherous and bitter than the men." In the previous July Captain Appleton had made the entry : If telegraph or railway is damaged within a certain radius, farm is burned. This seems severe, but it has been found that more lenient treatment was not sp. predated or respected. To give one instance. While one such farm was being burned near Paardekop, the lady of the house was weeping and gnashing her teeth and loudly protesting her innocence ; but the missing telegraph insulators from damaged veldt wires were found in her loft. The Boers are nearly all unreliabie and lie like the devil.

The ground Captain Appleton covers at length in hig " Diary "Lieutenant Lewis covers in interesting narra- tive form in his "Life at the Front " and Lieutenant Robson gives a vivid description of "A Day's Trek." The illustrations are very numerous, and include portraits of regimental cfficers and the company officers, of every man in the Ccmpany and the Third Contingent (still in South Africa), and ot the men who died on ; active service ; views of tho Company both at play and work, and of historic places which they visited ; ot General Buller visiting the camp at Ingaganc and of Colonel O'Leary's grave on Pieter' s 11111. Finally, the bock is handsomely bounu and would make a vcrr sensible Christmas present, being an instructive and pleasant account of a local act of patriotism which could be read with profit by all. The number printed is limited, so that those who are desircus of securing a copy should send order and P.O. at once to Captain Appleton, "Guardian" Office, Warrington ; Lieuteuant Lcwie, Ditton Lodge, Widnes ; or Sergeant Dutton, Cowley Hill, St Helene.

div.head: Strike of Brakesmen.
div.p: Strike of Brakesmen.

On Sunday morning a numb-ei-Oi.h.rakesmen em- ployed on the London and North-Western Railway at Wigan turned out on strike. Their grievance is that the trip rates paid them are inadequate,and do not admit of a fair wage. Tbey further complain of the pay for Sunday duty. The men refused to resume duty, and as a result of communications with Liverpool, Warrington and Crewe a number of brakesmen were sent to Wigan to take their places. Early on Monday morning Mr Dent, the superin- tendent of the Liverpool district,visited Wigan and interviewed the men, who stated their grievances, An understanding was arrived at, and the incident is regarded as closed.

Meeting of the Hounds at Appleton Hall. On Saturday a meeting of the North Cheshire hounds took place at Appleton Hall. Mr Wilson was in command. A start was delayed until noon owing to the hardness of the ground. The gardens surrounding the hall were without vulpine tenants. A fox ran out of Daresbury firs, but could not ba followed by reason of the frost. Grimsditch gave a quarry, which escaped after a six-fields bunt. A fifteen minutes' spin followed from Whitley by Seven Acre Wood to Dutton Hall farm, the fox being lost. A twenty minutes bunt from the same cover over poetically of the same line prefaced two blank draws, the day's operation then concluding.

div.head: QUEEN'S SOLDIER.
div.p: A QUEEN'S SOLDIER.
BY WALTER WOOD, Author of "Barrack and Battlefield," "Famous British Warships," "Through Battle to Pro- motion," "A Captain in the Fusiliers," "A Soldier of the Legion," &c,
CHAPTER XV.
ALONE ON THE VELD.

The patrol went steadily on at an easy walk. It was moving from the encampment near which Benn had been lying to another some miles further down the line; but of this the fugitive was unaware for several hours. All that he could do was to keep up his journey along the permanent way, following the patrol as closely as he could. For a consider- able time they rode very near the line, then Benn lost touch with them, but it was not long before the horsemen were parallel once more. He judged that from time to time it was needful for them to branch off from the railway because of the difficulty of riding; and from the close touch they main- tained with it, he assumed that they were out on work connected with the railway system. This he found to be the case. After covering, as it seemed to him, about ten miles, the patrol halted, and Benn found that another and larger Boer encampment had been reached, and that its object was the guarding of a vulnerable point of the railway. His wounded leg was now so painful that he seriously questioned his power to continue his flight; but he knew that to avoid recapture he would be forced to go ahead while the darkness remained, and find some secure place for conceal- ment during the day. He must, as far as possible, do his sleeping and planning by day, and his travelling by night. But it was imperative that he should halt and consider how he could best get past the encamp- ment. He sat down on the railway side, and took a draught from his water-bottle. He was hungry, too; but as there was no hope of relieving his craving for food, he tried to put the subject from his thoughts. Dogs were barking loudly, men were laughing and talking, horses were restless and noisy, and altogether there was so much commotion that Bann felt that the boldest plan would also be the safest —to push ahead as he had been doing, in the hope that he could slip through the encampment unobserved.

He rose once more, and, walking with as light a step as he could master, resumed his journey down the line, keeping on the side furthest from the encampment, and hiding as well as he could in the gloom. His chances of getting safely beyond the encamp- ment were small, for the light from the Boer fires was strong, and shewed the bright steel rails of the permanent way. Dogs, too, were prowling, and here and there were sentries, standing out, lonely and statuesque, in the red light. Altogether it seemed as if there was small chance of getting past the enemy in safety. But all the dangers of the encampment itself Mark passed through safely. He was already rejoicing at his luck when he noticed, very dimly, a figure in the darkness straight ahead of him. Only Mark's keen eyesight enabled him to see the figure at all, and then only well enough to make out that it was a man with a rifle, who was guarding the railway, walking to and fro across the line, with the obvious purpose of seeing that nothing unauthorised went to or came near the capital. Mark's position was perilous. There was a certainty of discovery if he continued his present course; and a great risk of capture if he left the line and tried to make his way across the open country. But there was one method which promised success, and that was to stalk the sentry, fall upon him unexpectedly, and by destroying or disabling him, make it possible to continue his flight. Beim was not in a mood to shrink from extremities, although at any other time he would have shuddered at the mere thought of an outrage like this. _ _

Advancing slowly, he noticed that the figure was no longer crossing and re-crossing the line. The discipline of the encampment was lax, the enemy was far away, and the sentinel, •being left to himself, had sought a soft spot on the railway side, facing the encampment, and had fallen into a com- fortable sleep. Crawling along in the shadow of an embankment, Benn got abreast of the sentry. A few steps more would have taken him in safety past, but an idea had entered his mind which made him pause. The sentry was leaning against a little bank of earth, his hat tilted over his brow, his legs stretched out, and his rifle across them, his right hand resting on the breech. In the light of the nearest fires it was just possible for the Yeoman to make out that the man was of heavy build and black-bearded, and that, tired and wounded as he was, Mark could have no hope of overcoming him in a personal encounter. But it had occurred to him that if he could seize the ,rifle and the ammunition of the sentry, his case might be less desperate, and that if driven to the veld he might be able to win his food with his gun. To have a weapon like that might make all the difference between life and death. It was this which caused him silently to make - his way to the sleeping figure, and with the swiftness of thought to strike him him on the temple with his hard-clenched fist. Mark shrank a little as he heard the thud of the blow, and saw the heavy head sink upon the breast. For a moment he thought, and feared, that the sentry was dead ; but the stertorou's breathing shewed that he was living. With a few quick movements, Mark possessed himself of the rifle and unstrapped the ammunition bandolier and put it round his own shoulders. Swiftly, too, he took a large, coarse handkerchief from; the sentinel's jacket and bound it round his mouth as a gag. Having done this and put the figure into the best position of ease and comfort that he could think of, and made certain that there was no fear of his injury from a passing train or of suffocation from the gag, Mark summoned all his energy and strength, and, resolutely forgetful of his weakness and suffering, ran clumsily adopt, the line, stopping for an instant now and then to look over his shoulder to see whether he was followed. Every step was torture, but Mark went on with what in merrier moments he would have called a hop and a kick. Every instant he expected to hear the thud of hoofs and the cries of men and the barks of dogs. In that case, the end was certain; he could expect no mercy at the hands of an infuriated enemy. There could be no possibility of establishing his innocence. As he thought of this, he remembered with a grim smile that he had a Mauser and a bandolier of cartridges, and that, as he understood the working of the weapon and was a good shot, besides being a desperate man, he could sell his life at an appalling sacrifice. On one point he was fiercely resolute: he would not now be recaptured living. But Benn continued his escape unmolested. Unable longer to run, he settled into a walk; then he slackened speed still, and went stolidly on down the line until he saw the day was breaking. Upon this he struck boldly from the line and gained the open country. He looked about him in the quickly growing light, and found that the railway he had left passed through a narrow cutting, a hill running parallel with a river. Careful not to show his out- line against the sky, he looked about him, and discovered in his rear, coming from the direction he had taken, a small body of horsemen, ten or a dozen in all—he could not be certain as to the exact number. It was clear from the way they rode and searched the ground, that they were pursuing him, and that unless he was exception- ally fortunate, he must be killed or retaken. For two or three minutes Ben, hidden in some high grass, lay prostrate on the ground, with his rifle presented, determined to pick off as many of the riders as he could before they were close upon him. As to his power to destroy the whole band he had no doubt; the only consideration that restrained him was the thought that the firing might bring other Boers to the spot, and thus make escape impossible. No sooner was this clear to Mark than he lowered his rifle and began to wriggle towards the river and there, finding some more high grass, he hid himself, his head being just above water, and himself invisible amongst the blades. The patrol halted, and made a thorough search of the railway, the land on each side and the banks of the river, hunting up and down repeatedly, and • their dogs working hard with them. It was from the animals more than the men that Mark feared discovery; but although more than once they were so near tli,.t he believed detection to be certain, ha was passed, and after a final search in a body, the patrol rode off and continued its march in the only direction which it was supposed Benn could have taken, and which, but for the pursuit, he would have been now following. For an hour after he had heard the last bark and the last shout, Mark kept motionless, He

had tried to Wel his rise above the water, but had failed; the bandolier, too, was so thoroughly soaked that he scarcely expected the ammuni- tion in it to be serviceable. With a heavy heart, therefore, Bonn let his Mauser slip and sink in the sodden grass, and unbuckled the bandolier and let that go also. The only consolation he had was the thought that with the loss of the rifle and belt of cartridges, there went what must have proved a very dangerouS piece of evidence against him, if recaptured. With them in his possession, his guilt would be clear, but free of them, who was to prove that he had struck or even seen the sentry? When it was no longer possible for him to endure his cramped position, Mark slowly raised himself, looked carefully about him over the top of the grass, and, being sure that there were no living creatures near, he pushed his way down the bank, and, seeing a likely spot for crossing, threw himself down to rest awhile, so that he might summon all his strength to swim across. Another hour passed, then Mark rose, and not without a fear of being unable to hold out until the other side was reached, he entered the water, and struck out for what looked like a reedy landing-place. Bonn was a strong, sure swimmer, and made his way without using his wounded leg. Changing from breast to side, and side to back, he got across, and landed amongst the reeds. Through these he crept until he reached the steep side of a hill, and, having climbed this and discovered a clump of bracken, he lay down in it, dripping and famishing, and felt that it would be a mercy if the Boers would come and take him. But his love of life was as great as his vitality, and the hot sun quickly dried his clothes and warmed his aching bones. He felt safe, too, amid the bracken, and before noon he had risen so that he could look about him.

Benn's sharp eye saw signs of man. He hurried from his hiding-place, forgetful for the time that he was in the midst of an enemy, and a deep expression of thankfulness escaped him when he noticed that the place had served as a temporary encampment for the Boers, and that scattered about the ground were scraps of food—meat and biscuit —while in an iron vessel like the three-legged cooking-pots they used at home was a quantity of coffee. _ _

Mark fell upon the broken food with ravenous enjoyment. The meat was doubtful as to freshness, and the biscuit had been roughly handled before being cast aside. The coffee, too, was thick and sweet, but all the same the meal was more to Benn than any banquet could have been in England. He ate and drank until he was perfectly satisfied, then with a thankful heart crept back to his bracken, and covering himself with the broad leaves, fell into a peaceful and refreshing sleep. Byway of making his enjoyment perfect he would have smoked a cigarette, but on bringing forth his precious packet he found that the tobacco was sodden, though the thin, tough paper still held it in the tiny rolls. The matches, also, were useless. Before closing his eyes Benn put the cigarettes and matches on the ground in the sun, knowing that they would soon be dry and fit for use. CHAPTER XVI.

div.head: BACK TO THE FARM.
div.p: BACK TO THE FARM.
I countless hours nTn re s sly cider(

- This alone almost determined him to continue his struggle ; but any further hesitation left him when he thought of Lizzie and the future. Things were bad, but surely there were many cases which were worse than his. He had been struggling for nearly a ,yeek. Could he not go on struggling still ?

I As these thoughts shaped themselves 'definitely in Benn's mind he became calmer and more resolute. He even raised himself from his prostrate position, sat up, and gazed about him. As he looked he heard a strange rumbling noise in the distance. For a moment he thought it was the sound of thunder, but the air was too clear and Cool for that to be possible, nor was there any sign of lightning. The idea that horsemen might be coming caused Mark to make an effort to raise himself upon his elbows to listen. The sound was rapidly coming nearer, and like a flash it occurred to Benn that it was made by an approaching train, and that he must be very near the railway. If this were so there was yet a shadowy hope of rescue, and with all his spirit returning at the prospect of salvation he staggered to his feet, and in black darkness groped his way towards the spot from which the noise approached. He could now see the headlights of an engine and hear the clank of a train. It was travelling very slowly and cautiously, and slackening 'speed as Benn drew nearer. It was easy to step from the veld to the metals and to stand on the side on which the train was coming. Benn was determined at all risks to shout and claim the notice of the driver, and in that way get picked up and taken on board. At the worst he could only be driven to the capital again and shot there; but even that would be better than the lonely death upon this awful veld. The train came nearer and more slowly. As it got abreast of Benn it was almost at a standstill. The figures of the driver and his mate stood out against the ruddy lire of the furnace, and Bean felt sure that they must see him. He waved his hands and cried "Hullo!" But the men saw nothing of him, and amid the noise of the train his voice, enfeebled by his sufferings so that it rose acarcely beyond a hoarse croak, was not heard. Benn cried again and waved his arms furiously; but by that time the engine had got a few yards beyond him and was slowly gaining speed, dragging the long body of trucks after it. With the strength of despair Benn rushed at the train. He could just make out that in fruit of him, passing away, was an open truck the top of 'which he could reach with his hands. He threw himself forward, seized the top, and as he was swept off his feet, managed with a desperate pull to raise himself.

Time after time he tried to raise himself high enough to tumble into the truck; and not until he was groaning with pain and despairing of success did he, with one final exertion, get his body douhled our thy edge of the truck. After that he

So far, Mark considered that he had been exceptionally fortunate. But with the resumption of his flight his good luck seemed to forsake him. First he found, on examination, that his clothing was little better than rags, and that his feet were so ill-covered that he might almost have been without hoots at all. his compass, too, had disappeared, having, he supposed, slipped from its resting-place while he lay in hiding on the river bank in the tall grass. But there was still the broken food, and this he packed about him as lavishly as he could manage to do. He ate another meal, and drank deeply from the river before re- starting at night, and having refilled his bottle he cast himself upon the veld, and hoped in good fortune to reach a place of safety. It seemed to him as if he walked on ground on which the foot of man or beast had never trod. Qf fellow-creatures he saw no signs ; but for this he was not sorry. No men were better than those who should prove to be enemies. Whenever he ' could get along at all, irrespective of day or night, Benn pushed ahead, keeping, as well as he could guess, to the point which the burgher had indicated. He suffered intensely in the daytime from the heat and in the night from cold; but day after day for six days he held inflexibly to his purpose. By that time he was in a state of prostration. It seemed to him as if he had been wandering for conntless, hours to _no_xurpose, and as if it was expressly ordered by fate that the end of his journey was never to be reached. His head reeled, his eyes swam ; he was no longer able to distinguish earth from sky or rising ground from level. Every- thing was one vast, grey, undistinguishable mass, and in a final fit of desPair he threw up his hands with a cry and fell face downward on the veld. He had no idea where he was. For many hours he ha 3 been wandering aimlessly in a region from which it seemed that no succour was likely to come. There was no sign of man, no trace of food or drink; nothing but barren monotony. He felt that now, indeed, the end was come, and that all that was left for him to do was to meet his fate with strength and calmness. His body was weary, his energy exhausted; for the moment his mental powers were enfeebled, and he only prayed that the end might come swiftly. The hot dust of the veld filled his month and eyes and nostrils. It irritated his body where it entered through the gaping rents of his clothing. But as Mark lay prostrate his will-power was revived, his exhausted powers became refreshed, and he found that the lust of life was as strong within him as ever. To die even on board ship, in prison at Water- - fall, in hospital amongst his own people, in skirmish or set engagement, that had not at any time seemed hard to him because he was a soldier; but it was more than he could endure to think that death should come upon him in this way, and that so long as he could crawl or drag himself upon the ground he should give up the fight. He thought of all that men had gone through since the war began, of those who, hour after hour, had been forced to lie in bitter cold upon the ground, wounded and helpless, and who, by resolute spirit, had kept themselves alive till help came. Many such cases lie had heard of, cases, too, in which the men had lived to go back to the front and take their places afresh in the fighting line.

managed to gain the inside, and the safety of the hard, uncomfortable floor. He was full of energy and keenness once more, and rejoiced intensely when he found that the train was steadily jogging ahead. It did not again pull up or stop for a full hour, and then Mark heard the driver talking with some man who had walked up from the side of the track. What the talk was about Mark could not understand, but it was, he judged, of a serious and warning character. He was puzzled, too, to under- stand why an empty goods train should be running in such a very mysterious fashion. The train resumed its journey, and did not stop again until a little station was reached which to Mark had a familiar air. Through a crevice in the Bide of the truck he could see figures moving rapidly about, and became aware of hurry and intense excitement. With a jerk, the train began to move backwards as if shunting. Mark saw that now or never he must leave his hiding-place. It was still dark, and there seemed to be no one near him. The guard from his van in the rear had gone ahead and was waving a lamp to the driver as a signal to go ahead again. Without an instant's hesitation, Benn clambered over the rear of the truck, stepped on to the buffer nearest to the other set of rails, and jumped. Hei made a heavy fall, but rose to his feet and hurried down the line in the direction from which he had come. When the train was well past him, he crossed the metals and got clear of the railway. A. moment's examination chewed him that he was back at the little station near which Boota's farm lay, and that a Boer encampment which had been formed there was being broken up in haste. Men were tumbling into trucks, horses were being hurried aboard, and, judging, from sounds which reached him from the rear of the vehicles, desperate efforts were being made to entrain some field guns. The engine had by this time been shunted to what had been the rear of the train, and the train itself pulled on to the set of metals leading to Pretoria. This much Mark understood from his previous knowledge of the station, and he assumed that British troops were very close at hand. Such a belief encouraged him enormously, and developed those military instincts which he had fostered since his enlist- ment. He took it to be his duty to learn all he could about this strange movement of the enemy, so that at the proper time he could make known what he had seen and heard to a superior authority. He calculated, roughly, how many horses, guns, and men had been encamped and were leaving, and listened hard to catch any scrap of conversation which could be of service to himself, as chewing how near the British were, and what prospect there was of a successful advance for them. But it was little he had learnt by the time the train went. Men spoke in a language which was strange to him, and spoke, too, in jerky, muffled sentences. Even if they had talked in English, it would have been hard to follow them; but now, with noise and bustle on every side, and using a foreign tongue, it was impossible to grasp their meaning. Mark had to be content with drawing inferences from what lie had seen, and he judged that the enemy was hurrying with all speed from the place of encampment and falling back upon Pretoria. _ (2'o, be continued.)

div.head: JEST AND ITS SEQUEL. ---- Blackburn Weaver's Chance Remark.
div.p: A JEST AND ITS SEQUEL. ---- Blackburn Weaver's Chance Remark.

It is a time-honoured aphorism that many a true word is spoken in jest, but seldom, indeed, is it that the sequel of a jest has been fraught with so much import- ance as the following case. The innocent jest referred to was made by Mr Jackson, 21, Fernhurst-street, Ewood, Blackburn, and the important consequences that followed that chance remark were detailed to a " Blackburn Standard " reporter by his wife. " How did it all come about ?" was the reporter's first question. 66 Well," said Mrs Jackson, " when I was married six years ago I was then ia a very poor state of health. I began slowly but surely to grow worse and worse. I had a severe attack of influenza some Lima previously, which dragged ma down to an exceeding weak state. and it seemed as though I was never to recover enough at ength to get about without feeling utterly exhausted. The r fleet on my spirits was serious, for I could not shake off the intense melancholy which had become part of my life. I was always miserable, and could only look at the dark side of everything." " You sought medical advice, I presume ?'' "Yes, of course ; but the doctors told me little except that my complaint was a general weakness, and that my kidneys were affected. This state of melancholy told on my appetite and digestive powers, and for a long time retail treated also to indigestion without feel- ing the smallest relief. I seemed to grow worse every day, although I still trudged to work cub morninC feeling half dead. The weavers at the mill where I worked used to wonder what had come over me, and I was urged to give up two of the four looms I was runn- ing, for I was like a ghost. All the colour had left my cheeks, and I used to tell my husband that I would not live much longer. I had no appetite ; food used to sicken me, and I got properly downhearted. My friends besought me to try first one doctor and then another, but to tell you the truth I had lost heart and cared little what _happened."
" You'appear to take an interest in life now," inter. rupted the reporter, " judging by your appearance, which is anything but ghost-like."

Yes," said la; Jacliiion.:who was present during the I interview, " my wife looks healthy enough now doesn't I ite ? Perhaps it will he as well if I explain. It's due to me and Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people that Imy wife is now cured and looking so well. I saw the pills advertised in the newspaper, and jestingly said to her. 'Well, you had better get some of these pills. They are for pale people, and you are pale enough anyhow 1 got some, more to carry out my joke than anything and she took two or three pills every day. I am not I jesting when I tell you that she was better in a I week, and her relatives were surprisel and said ' Whatever's making our Annie's colour come back ? ' But what was more important than the colour ot her ' cheeks was the return of health and strength, and a lively interest in life. Tile rapid change was wonder- ful."

"Then you- honestly believe the cure to be due en- tirely to Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people, and you are quite willirm the public Would have the benefit of your experience ? " "Of course," replied Mrs Jackson, " and I tell everybody to take them. They bave saved my life and pounds in dectors' bills," Mrs :Jackson runs 'four looms atNessrs Liveser'a Ewood Mill, Blackburn, and to use her own words, he was never in better health in her life, and avows her husband's joke has turned out a real blessing in disguise.

WARRINGTON. Improvements at the "Hop Pole" Hotel. At the Coun4 Borough Police Court on Monday, 1 Mr T S Steel made an application on behalf of the Bedford Brewery Company, for permission to carry out certain alterations to the "Hop role "Inn. The plans, he said, had already been before the Watch Committee, and the Chief Constable had also seen - them. The hotel was adapted some years ago for • the purposes of a music licence, but this had been suppressed, and the place was now no suitable for the present arrangements. He described the altera- tions. Part of the living rooms was now down- stairs. It was proposed to kave all the living rooms upstairs. It was also proposed to have stairs lead- ing from the smoke room to the club room. At present people going to the club room had to pass the bedrooms. Adequate lavatory accommodation would be provided downstairs.—The Chief Con- stable said be had examined the plans and visited the house.—Mr Steel pointed out that the new arrangement would decrease the drinking area by' about 30 square yards.—The Chief Constable said the living rooms downstairs might be and were, when the house was full,' used for drinking pur- poses. The arrangement was most objectionable, especially where there were children. Of course, there was no doubt the brewers suggested this re- arrangement for the purposes of increasing their trade. They did not do that sort of thing to decrease their trade. The new arrangement would, however, facilitate police supervision of the house.—ln reply to the Chairman (Mr I` ,IS.lonks), Mr Steel said the yard was self-contained and the big doors in florsemarket-street were always kept closed. The application was granted.
