MUNICIPAL TRADING CONTROVERSY.
Thursday Night's Meeting of
Ratepayers.
Mr. Pemberton Accepts Alderman Roberts's Challenge.
-- Charges Against Other members of the Council.
-- Mr. Norbury Williams and H. Ingram Limited.

Parr Hall was packed to its utmost capacity on Thursday last week, when a further meeting of the ratepayers and others "in favour of no municipal trading direct or indirect, by members of the Cor- poration," was held. Long before the time announced for the meeting to Commence people were flocking to the hall, and by the time the proceedings opened every available Space including, the platform wee occupied A great many Who Were anxious to obtain admit- tance had to be turned away. The chair was again taken by Mr James Dodds, and he was supported by Messrs Norbury Williams ( elanchester), E L Fleming, Septimus Kenyon, John Pem- berton, S Gough, Nightingale, and A Hulme. The Crietaleeet, who was warmly received, seid teat before he asked Mr. Fleming, their secretary, to read sorne letters which he had received, he wiseed to tell them exactly what the order of procedure would be, After he had spoken the resolution asking for an enquiry into the last five years' trading with the Corporation by members of the Council, and condemning all such improper trading would be submitted. Questions in 'writing which were sent up to himland which were approved by him wouid be answered, but as that was a meeting solely for those in sympathy with their objects—(heare hear)—no irrelevant questions or speeches in opposition to their objects would be allowed. He was quite sure every gentleman present would assist him in observing order, and he hoped tie might have no necessity—as he did not think he would —to ask the assistatice of the officers of the law who were present. If be bad such necessity be was desired by Inspector Phillips, who was in an adjoining room, to say he had an ample number of officers to quell any interruptioo. He would HOW ask Mr. Fleming to read the letters that had been received. " AKE YOU IN FAVOUR OF A THOROUGH ENQUIRY ? " THE REPLIES OF COUNCILLORS. Mr. E. L. FLEMING, secretary of the Committee, ssid the following question had been put by Mr. Dodds to all the members ot the Ceuecil .—" Are you in favour of a thorough enquiry ?" Eleven answers had been received by Mr Dolls. Eight of the Town Cluncillors were in favour of a thor- ough investigation : one was against.—Mr A J Jolley : one was for it if the Council thoueht it was necessary, and one wag for it if Mr Norbury Williams was kept out (" oh " I and laughter.) I letter bad been receive 1 from Mr Cameron, SI P. addressed to Mr Dodds. The letter stated that Mr Cameron would be engaged every day for three weeks except when he was travelling. Re was sorry not to be able to " come to your help ; later we will give you a lift." (Applause). Mr Fleming then read the folio sing letters : Councillor T J HULSE Wrote :—" Replying to your cir- cular, I beg to state that I have no objection whatever to an enquiry being made such as named by you." Councillor SMETHURST wrote :—" In answer to your letter of the late, I new say I am in favour of any in- vestigation which may be consilered necessary." Councillor WILLIAM ROBERTS wrote :—" In reply to your letter, I wish to say that if your committee will make definite charges against the members of the Town' Council whose conduct they objeot to, I shall be quite I willing to consent to an impartial enquiry taking place. At the same time I shall strongly oppose a man like Norbury Williams taking part in it, because he has pro- nounced judgment without hearing both sides." (Laughter and booing). Councillor WILKINSON wrote in favour of a thorough Investigation. Councilor Baotron wrote :—" I cordially agree with the underlying principle for which you are contending. I shall always do both in the Council and out of it whatever I can to preserve the purity of public moral- ity, and nothing that is unfair and not above board will ever receive either my synapatey or support. I Support Mr Tinnion in welcoming a thorough investi- gation of the allegations respecting the improper trad- ing on the part of councillors and aldermen of the borough." Councillor W PIERPOINT wrote :—" le it as evidently the opinion of a large number of ratepayers that mem- bers of the Town Council have been and are improperly tradinz with the Corporation, it is only my duty to acknowledge their right to a complete and full in- quiry." (Hear. hear). Councillors FORSHAW and Bone or: wrote in favour of an levity. Councillor Joliet ROBERTS wrote :—" I am not aware that there is any improper trading between the alder- men and councillors and the Corporation, and, if there is any, I am decidedly in favour of an investigation as the wisest means of bringing such strange allegations to an end. Ever since I have been a councillor, I have coneiderel myself a servant of the ratepayers, and what is their interest is also mine." Mr FLEMING geld Councillor Plumpton was in favour of an investigation being made, and there wag a long letter from Councillor A Jelollay to which Mr Norbury Williams would reply later on. TOWN CLERIC DOES NOT UNDERSTAND. • The Towle CLERK (Mr J Lyon Whittle) wrote :—" I am in receipt of your letter of the 15th inst., enclosing copy of a circular which you have sent to the mem- bers of the Council. I do not understand why you have sent the copy circular to me." Me FLEMING informed the meeting that they had told the Town Clerk that the circular had been Sent to hint Simply as a matter of courtesy. MR. U. R. PEARSON AND TITE LETTING OF PARR HALL. Mr FLEMING concluded by stating that Mr R H Pear- son wished it to be known that he had not received any commiselon on the letting of the Parr Hal to the ratepayers for the last meeting, as a statement was being circulated which was calculated to damage him. He had been requested to state that if there was any- one affected or intimidated or intimidation offered to anytone ratepayer on their Side, if •he would let the committee know they would take the matter up and defend it. (Applause.) THE CHAIRMAN DENOUNCES MUNICIPAL TRADING. THE NEW MAYOR AND FE&RSON AND KNOWLES. , The CHAIRMAN then addressed the meeting. He said: sess than a short month has elapsed since the election ct the tee , Committee of Warrington ratepayers charged by .e.p.earge public meeting held in the Co-operative Hall vu the specific dutt of bringing to an end at the Cr, Possible moment the considerable, the highly tracunPer, the immoral, and, in some cases, the illegal I? which has been vine on for years between member teeete aof the Warrington Town Council and the War- Seen' 'll Corporation Yet in that short time we have so em progress ; we have had a change of Mayors (aw , etlee)—and the political compact—that unholy all a 0 evil effects of which the people of War- rington have suffered from, and Must suffer from for years to come, has been scotched, and if not killed has been wounded unto death. (Hear, hear). When the committee was formed we were within 18 hours of the West time for receiving nominations for the nine vacant Seats in the Council, yet we were able to take such action as resulted in at least seven of the re-elected - • members accepting our platform in regard to any Muni•• cipal trading, either personally or through Limited Companies, while in regard to the seat we contested, despit3 the frantic efforts of many prominent but dis- loyal members of Mr Pemberton's party in the Town Council and outside, he waged a contest with a result which, teough unsuccessful, astonished the opponents of his gallant fight for purity in public life. (Cheers.) Coming to the re-election of Aldermen we were astounded to find that every retiring Councillor was pledged in writing to the re-election of the retiring Aldermen, and not only so but was also pl Aged to only , vote into the position of Aldermen the senior Councillors When I heard of this pledge I realized at once that it would be improper to press the retiring candidates to break their written pledges, and though I suggested to them that the wishes of the electors as expressed at the two large meetings ought to overrule the pledges given, I could not and did not urge them further. From the • report of the last Meeting of the Council, you al wel see that Councillor Tinnion Stated the terms of e Pledge every member had signed from and since Novem- • ber 9th, 1897. It is a fact, but it is to my mind a most improper thing, that when neW Illenlbers Of the Council sign their acceptance of office, they have put before them at the same time and by the Town Clerk', a document in the form of s pledge in regard to the election and re-election of Aldermen. Now what are the terms of this document—l mean of this pledge —which was signed by every member of the Town Council on November 9th, 1897, and which has been Signed by every member on his election to the Council Since? Here they are :—" We the undersigned members ot the Warrington Town Council hereby respectively agree to observe the rule of seniority amongst the members of the Council in the election or re-election of the Present or future Aldermen of the borough." Mark, gentlemen, the unmistakable meaning of that niedee. It is an absolute insurance of an aleermanie office for ife—for life, mind you—fer every present Alderman, and it is moreover an absolute obstacle to any ex- ceptionally able man being elected an alderman from in !tele or outside the Couneil,except in the order of 'senior- . ItY in the Council: Could anything be more ridiculous ? ,e there anything more d awning to the existing regime? another result Of that notorious Compact, now I believe
I

so far as the respectable leaders and the rank and file o both political parties are concerned, as dead as Qaeen Anne. Let nee ask your attention once more in passing to the election of the five alderman on the 9M instant. You will remember that Councillor TlaGioo, after read- ing the pledge I have just referred to, went on to say that "he could not see how in view of the pledge) any body of men could expect 'them as honourable men, having signed the document and knowing so well its contents, to go against their word. He should consider that any member who voted otherwise in the circum- stances would be guilty of a gross breach of honour to his colleagues." . . . Therefore that was the reason be (Councillor Titmice') intended to vote for the re-elec- tion of "the retiring aldermen." Now notice THE REMARKS OF ALDERMAN ROBERTS in acicnowleging the re-election, a re-election to which the members were bound by the solemn and formal pledge I have alluded to, and with Ceuncillor rinnion's pistol at their heads so to speak. Alderman Roberts said the vote (forced, mind, you, from the members in the way I have described) " was some reply to the unnecessary and scandalous charges which had been circulated during the past four weeks! " How many votes would have been given for the re-election had there been a free vote I shall not attempt to guess. (Hear, hear.) One word, and one word only, as to these alleged Vandstous charges. Let me ask Alderman Roberts to calmly realize what is the charge against him so far as I have made it. It is that he has, through the Warrington Slate Compaay,traded largely with the Cor- poration, and that although such trading is legal it is highly improper. What is his reply ? I; is that all trading through the Slate Company is legal—that the direct contract is improper hence he will,he says,accept no more profit far himself and family from this source ; that the sub-contracting is proper, and finally, as you heard him state at the last meeting here, that all the trading will go on. Therefore Alderman Roberts says, in eect that aly charging him with doing what he says is both legal and proper is a scandalous chaige. If what he is doing is legal and proper, how can he consider it scandalous for me to state the same premises, and to express a contrary opinicie as to their propriety. The introduction of the offensive word I have jast qa3ted was entirely 'milled for, and I now leave you to settle for yourselves as to whose conduct the term " scandal- ous," so glibly and freely used by the late Mayor, can be most fitly applied, if it can be s o applied at all. I don't say it can. The undesirable position of the Managing Director of the Warriaeton State Company. Limited, could hardly be better shown, than by putting THE WARRINGTON SLATE COMPANY into the position of the Corporation. L9'.; us suppose that the Warrington Slate Company beugn; very largely from a firm, and Mr Roberts as head of the Slate Company, discovered that the manager of the Slate Company held 5-Bths of the shares in the firm so supplying the Slate Company, would Mr Roberts say that his manager was in a right pesitien ? Woald he not send him to the right about. But that is the posi- tion of Mr Roberts iaow, as a trustee and offi ter of the Corporation and that is why we say he should either trade with Ale Corporation from outside, or if he wants to be a member of the Cerperatien he should give up trading with it. In this connection I wish, for obvious reasons, to refer to my first letter on this subject of. municipel trading published six months ago. In it I clearly indicated that I should not be the man to take exception to the case of a Member of the Town Council, who was a small shareholder, but not an offieer, in a great concern which -did a small business with the Corporation, and I stand tonight, exactly where I did 6 months ago in that r wee:, although for my own part, if I were to seek to enter the Council I should feel it to be my duty to divest myself of any and all interests whatever, however small, in any Cempany doing only the smallest amount of business with the Cor- poration. (Cheers.) In THE CASE SAY OF OUR NEW MAYOR or of Mr. Councillor Forshaw. we° both hold insignifi- cant holdings as shareholders only, in very large local manufacturing concerns, they must jadge for them- selves ; but in the case such as Ingrains Limited. the Warrington and District Electric Light and Power Com- pany, Limited. and J. Buckley and Company, Limited, where the holdings of Councillors, though smell, bear a high proportion to the small total capital, where the profits are likely to be excessive, where it is possible, if ant probable, the companies have been constituted -with nn eye mainly for Corporation business, and where such Councillors are officers of the Companies—l hold that such Councillors or Aldermen are in an entirely wrong position, and Minna retire, either from the companies, or from the Corporation. (Cheers). Let me now deal with the laesst puny suggestion of some puny mind. In sending out the circular to the members of the Council asking them if they were favourable to a thorough investigation into the im- proper trading by members of the Council our com- mittee felt that it would not be courteous to the new Mayor, who had only jolt been elected from out dele the Council, and who =id not be fairly called up on so early to decide upon his action, to send him a circular. Ills suggested that because the Mayor still holds a few shares in Pearson and Knowles—his present holding re- presents less that a two-thousandth part of the capital of that Company, that I as an officer of that Company, of which I am proud, was afraid to send a Copy of the ircular to the Mayor. Gentlemen, I resent eller COWARDLY INSINUATION, and I say that if I thought that. Mr Cnarlton Parr, or any other man, whatever his association with me, was in an improper position in regard to a question of public morality, I snould not hesitate, if duty called for it, to impeach him at the bar of public opinion. (Cheers.) I am sorry to have to notice these paltry suggestions, these dying efforts in a lost cause. Gentlemen, how easy it is for a man who has embarked upon devious courses to anonymously suggest diffieulties in the way of right doing. If such mama now wanted to do the right, there would be no difficulty whatever, as I have already clearly indicated. A true and an honourable man knows instinctively, so to speak, where and when the wrong begins ; it is only the other man who pre- tends he cannot see, who needs the check of preventive and punishing laws. I have now to refer to a letter I have had from Mr Councillor A J Jolley, and which, I assume, he wishes me to answer. He is, I believe, a well-meaning gentleman, and is very much exercised in regard to my loss of reputation as a result of my having joined the Committee for stopping all improper naunici- pal trading.. He writes " I have no desire to say any- thing discourteous to yourself, and am fully aware that in any considerable public movement an honourable man may be compelled to act with associates inspired With lees creditable motives than his own, but I think your CallSl and in some measure your personal reputa- tion, have suffered from permitting Mr Norbury Williams to come forward as one of your champions." I observe also that the Warrington " Observer," and in a lesser degree, the Warrington "Examiner," are very fond of referring to the Combination of DoddS and Co., of Pemberton, Gough, Dodds and Co., of Dodds, Flem- ing and Co. and so on.-4 have no doubt" Jolley,Dodds and Co." would sound more euphonious, more agreeable to the ear, and to the . ideas of the gentlemen who are responsible for the " Examiner " and " Observer " notes, but I say that Mr Jolley and the Conservative and Liberal °roans in Warrington, have all, unfortunately as I think, and if I may use a slang expression, " put their money on the wrong horse," and one of these fine days they will wake up " wiser and sadder men." No,gentle- men, if these parties think that I am to be moved from the course upon which I have embarked in regard to this question, if they think I am the man to trim my sails to every passing breeze, if they think that by threate of damaged reputation they can divert me from a course dictated by my hoad,heart and conscience they have reckoned without their host. Our issue in this campaign is an upright administration of the muni- cipal affairs of Warrington, conceived and executed solely for the benefit of the people. (Cheers.) It is the issue of common honesty. It is the fight of good citizenship, against bed, selfish,and careless citizenship, and the contest naturally divides itself into two parts, first the securing of a thorough investigation in regard to the illegal and improper trading of the past, and secondly and chiefly, the creation of a public sentiment which shall at the earliest possible moment drive from the Council Chamber every man who benefits directly or indirectly, through himself • or through limited com- panies, and every man who allows any other man to do so. (Cheers.)

div.head: SIR. BRADSHAW AND INGRAMS, LIMITED. SHARES ON SALE.
div.p: SIR. BRADSHAW AND INGRAMS, LIMITED. SHARES ON SALE.

The Enamor/or said he had received the following letter from Mr Edwin Bradshaw, one of the elective auditors : Dear Sir,—Adverting to the let•er cf Mr Nmbury Williams in the public press of Saturday last containing a reference to my bolding 25 shares in H Ingram Ltd.' I desire to make the assurance, that these snares were acquired by me ia perfect go 3d faith and without the slightest thought or idea that my positim as an Elective Auditor of the Borough readared such acquisition in the faintest degree objectionable or undesirable. Neverthe- less I now quite see it is possible that in some minds it may be csnsidered at least inadvisable in however small a degree that I should hold such shares having regard to my official position as auditor. I have therefore decided that the public are entitled to any doubt which ecTri the most fastidious may entertain as to my position in the matter and have accordingly instructed my broker to at once dispose of the shares in order that I may be absolutely free from the slightest taint or suspicion of self-interest in the mind of the public or any part of it. It must be clearly understood, however, that by so doing Ido not admit that my holding was eitaer illegal or even remotely con- trary to good morals, and it is absurd to suppose that such a holding would influence me to the prejudice of the interests of the ratepayers ; I do not wish to engage in newspaper controvery and thinking the matter may possibly be referred to at the Meeting to-night it occurs to me to be proper that you should have this letter and explanation before you. —Yours truly. EDWIN BIaDSIIVir. THE RESOLUTION. TRUST DEAD IN WARRINGTON. Mr ALFRED HULAS% in moving a resolution similar to that passed at the last meeting, said that members of the Town Council asked the ratepayers to take them on

ever read the wording of. The men who had entered during the last four years had absolutely been such weak-kneed creatures as to sign their liberty away before they had been a single hour in the Town Hall. How could they expect strong action from men who were so weak, so contemptibly weak as that ? So far as he could make out the Corporation appeared to transact business with hardly anybody but limited com- panies. It was the most marvellous collection, should he say of wild beasts, that he had ever come across in the municipal line. (Laughter.) He had a great deal to say &befit these limited companies,but he had tried to get something from Alderman F W Monks who had been eleven years in the Council. He could not get anything out of Alderman Monks. (A voice: We can.) He had asked him about thirty questions and he had not answered one of tbem. How could he go on corres- ponding with a man of that sort? He had told him (Mr Williams) that he knew nothing, he (Mr Williams) asked him a few questions, Aldermaa Monks rushed to the paper, telegraphed to him that he was going to do it, sent his last letter to the paper and said " I have done with that correspondence." (Laughter.) Be (the speaker) had had a large experience in public life, but that beat everything in the way of correspondence that he had ever been involved in. Tee retirement of Alderman Monks was one of the extraor- dinary things of this twentieth century. (Laughter,) reference to the Warrington Slate company,they had been repeatedly told, and it had never been denied, that Alderman Henry Roberts held 88?. shares and his wife and children held a beaker 110, and that the total shares in that company were 1,725. If they divided 1,725 by 932, the number of shires held in the family of the Roberts's, they would find it was 57 par cent (Ironical whistles). Alderman Roberts and his family bossed" the company, there was no getting over that. There were many things that could be twisted but he'd be hanged if they could twist figures. If Mr Parr, who had made a great reputation and bad not a stain on his [I public or private character, wanted to retain that high name he must not be found at the head of a Corporation that did this crooked trading, or he would go out of office with a name less brilliant and less famous than Chat with which he recently entered office. He was not doubting Ph Charlton Parr. He believed he would rise to the position, and not being himself involved in half-a-dozen " limiteds " would say " Warrington shall make a new start." elk voice : "He is in them.")There:was one concern he must say a word about, because he had received a lawyer's letter about it which he would read to them. It refer- red to what he had said as to H Ingram, Limited, and he was sorry that two papers in Warrington, were not bold enough to print what ha said about it. A man who had been 25 years in this sort of work did not, as a rule, make a statement which he could not back up. Before he said what he did about H Ingram Limited he had every bit of evidence in writing (" Question.") In his correspondence he distinctly said in reference to that firm that all he alleged against it had taken place since their last meeting (A voice : "Question " and cries of "Chuck him out ") and that it bad happened under the very nose of the chairman of the Electricity Committee, Alderman F W Monks,who, he ascertained from inquiry was a 0100 honourable and estimable gentleman. Toe following was the latter he had received:—" Sir, your statementithat an offleisl of Ingram'a Ltd,called upon A B and Compaey on the 17th of October soon after a meet- ing of the electricity committee and solicited an order for motors and that be had obtained :information from an official of the Corporation is an unmitigated lie and if not withdrawn you may hear more about it." (Cheers and laughter.) He had not withdrawn it and he was not going b withdraw woat he said. (Cheers). The name of the solicitor—could they guess it ? (Cries of " Roberts.") It was F R Reberts, (Hooting.) Now it was very unfortunate, but he had got the documents there. That was the queer thing. Ingram's Limited had written a letter in which they said that no application for power had ever been made to the Corporation by A B and Company. Now it Wa3 a queer thing, but there was a letter he would just read to them. Mr Williams then read the letter which he said was addressed to the firm of A B and Co. as follows:—" H Ingram, Limited, electrical and mechanical engineers, 72, Sankey-street, Warring- ton, November sth, 1901. Gentlemen,—Hearing that you have made an application to the Warrington Corporation to fix motors at your place for motive power, and having fixed a considerable number of motors in and out of town, we shall be pleased to give you prices for any sizes that you may require at any time." (A voice: Mr. Sleekly). They would all know the name if the Cor- poration held this inquiry. What he objected to and always should object to was that the firm of H. Ingram, Limited, should receive information from the Corpora- tion or some of its officials which was not given to other firms in the same line. It was a scandal and it was a dis- grace. ( k Voice ; "It's a lie." Cries of "out with him.") He would prove every thing he had said. (Cheers.) If Mr F R Roberts wanted to lose a little money, which he would do, he could tell them—(Voices "He won't ")—he would do if he started this case. (A voice : "He won't start.") They said he would not Start. He thought all the Roberts's had started and had gone a good way. This was a miserable threat, and there had beets quite enough threats in Warrington till he was sick of threats. If any of hist hearers were threetemeceney must send an intimation to the com- mittee who would see that they were properly defended. He challenged Mr F R Roberts, whoever lie was—he heard 119 was a member of the Council—if he thought he (Mr Williams) had said anything which could not be proved to the hilt in every detail to let them have it out. (Loud cheers). Be had fought bigger men than Mr F R Roberts. (Cheers and laughter). If he believed a thing was true he was going to say it and if he be- lieved the Corporation was wrong, and he had absolute written proof of it, not all the F R Roberts's that were ever created were going to put any fright into him. Let them leave Roberts, he was sick of hearing tee name of Roberts. Another company had sprung up. He had had the p irticelers only that, day. It was called the Zillah Shipping and Carrying Company. This Company carried a lot of materiels used by the Corporation of Warrington, so he thought ha would like to see who were concerned in the com- pany which carried their gravel from Penmeenmawr and also setts front that same neighbourhood. He thought it strange if he should look through the list of this company and not find somebody in, because this Company had recently been carrying a lot of stuff whieh had been used on their tramways. He was not deceived. Tne first name he found was Councillor W Brough, 491 £5 shares, Chairman of the Cempany ; secondly, Alderman J Shaw Green, 154 £5 shares ; thirdly, Alderman II Roberts, 178 shares. Another thing had been put before him that day and it was this. A number of their friends in Warrington had conscien- tiously been opposed to them in tneir action. Their poiut of view had been placed before him and he thought it should be placed before them. A number of burgesses in Warrington were interested in this net- work of companies, and by this means and through this fact their minds has become warped. Continuing,he said they had opened their campaign but they would per- haps not have another meeting for several months. They should, however, have several next September and October, and there were nine men he wanted them etmoo enkace came de their bu yp efayoserk election nlnpze ttforho anti nnh eet nt peNax ott vt ehlmal right 3 rm. o t months. an ni aThesesmat the next election of auditors. The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried without dissent, and the meeting closed.

trust. The time for trust had gone past—trust was dead in Warrington. (Cum.) S KENTON seconded. tie remarked that the Cor- poration hadaot acted as though they would welcome an enquiry. Mr PEmBERToN, who had an enthusiastic reception, said he would like to say a word or two in regard to the recent Latchford election. It was alleged against him during teat election that he was crying to get a position on the Council in order that he might be able to sell bricks to the Corporation. (1, voice : "No chance," and laughter). As that gentleman Ina said, he would have no chance, even if he had desired to do such a thing. It was a significant fact that all the bricks used by the Warrington Corporation for many years were Gm:agate bricks. It was a very good brick, but tura were half a dozen makers of equal merit. They could; however, only buy it in Warriagton from one firm, and that was the Warriagtoa Slate Company. (Laughter sad applause). During the Latchford elec- tion there were several geatlemen wee eh a wad great activity in working against him, and base insinua- tions were made which had no foundation in fact. The speaker proceeded to refer to a speech of the Deputy-Mayor made on the 30h October in which he said that years ago he put out a challenge that he would give £lOO to the Infirmary "if any single case of abuse or advantage that had been sought or obtained by me for myself or for nay firm would be proved by anybody." He (Mc Pemberton) was going to have a try fur that £lOO, and he publicly 'challenged Alderman Roberts to hear him on the subject, and he asked that Mr Wainwright, one ot the most eminent arbitrators they had in England should be asked to art:Ante on the question. (Cheers.) Mr Pemberton went on to refer to the statement of Alderman Roberts that the acceptance of the tenders of toe Slate Company had been to the advantage of the property own •r and ratep iyer te the extent of 101 per cent on the total outlay, and said that it that was the case not only could they get orders from Warrington, but from the whole of the United Kingdom, Alluding tto Committer A. J. Jolley, Mr. Pemberton thought Mr. Jolley looked after his own interests a bit because he was trying to sell to the Board of Guardians some property he was interested in, and the price he wanted for it would amount to £4,000. Ito his (Mr. Pernbertoa's) opinion it was not worth more than £2,000. He was not surprised at Mr. Jolley'a iatereat-- A Voice : No personal attacks. (Interruption). The Cratiacian : Our opponents complain that we deal in generaiities rani do not make personal attacks. We want to give specific cases and then our friend says "No personal attacks." (Hear, hear.) A Voice : Sick to the pint. Mr. PEMBERTON : I have been asked for the personal attacks. Proceeding, he said Messrs Greening and Sons had received from the Warrington Corporation two sums amounting to £62 103, and £250 respectively. What for? He did not know. He wanted to know but the Berough Treasurer said he was not entitled to know it, (Laughter.) He would like to say a few words about the position of the "Observer. It had astonished a great many people in Warrington, He had read a letter written by Mr A Stanway in connection with the "Obeerveras"position on this contract question.ildr Pem- berton proceeded to read the letter which appeared in ' lase Saturday's " Observer " as well as the footnote by the editor. Continuing, Mr Pemberton, said he would like to point oat that at the first meeting held in the Co-operative Hall on this municipal trading question,Mr Dodds mentioned that Mr L Tunstalt had received a pension from the Corporation of £361 a year. Many people outside the Council and a few in it kicked against it but it was rushed through. Not only had Mr Tunstall received the t pension but it seemed as though he had gone on receiving all the work the Corporation could put in their (Ifessrs Tunstall's) way. They went down to London and received a large amount of money as witnesses before the Local Government Board or the House of Commons Committee, he did not know which. In the case of Briggs, the last arbitration case with the Corporation, ono of the firm, Mr Thomas Tunstall appeared as a valuer for the Corporation, and Mr John Tunstall appeared in the same case as account- ant. Well, when he saw all other valuers and all other accountants passed over he thought it very peculiar so he wrote for a list of the directors and shareholders of the "Observer " company. He found Mr Thomas Tunstall was a director of the " Observer " ; he found Mr John Tunstall was a director of the" Observer," and ' Mr John Tunst all was also secretary. Be would leave ' that with the public. (Laughter ) It was said that they on the platform insinuated. The Observer" had been full of insinuations. He (Mr Pemberton) charged Alderman Sutton with illegal and immoral trading with ' the Corporation. A. Voice : " No personalities" and interruption. Cries of" Put him out.' 1 The CH&IRMAN : I should be very sorry— Mr PENIBERToN . Gentlenaen—Gentlemen—l charge , Alderman Francomb with illegal and immoral trading with the Council. I charge Shaw Green with illegal ' and inttnoral trading with the Council. I charge Harry , Roberts with immoral trading with the Council. I charge F R Roberts with immeral trading with the ' Council. I charge Alfred J Jolley with immoral trad- ing with the Council. Now gentlemen if that is not diStlnet, • proprr.. and straight, tall me what is. (Applause.) Mr NomaUrry Wiaraams, who had a flattering recep- tion. said that since they met in that hall, about three weeks ago, many things had happened, more things than ever happened ia Warringtoa in the same time be- fore, more conversions, more openings of the minds of the burgesses than was ever before produced in the ' brief space of 22 days. But there was one eveat which had happened and which he hoped might be of ; good augury, and that was that there had come into the Mayoral seat of this Borough, a man who had no municipal antecedents, who had no past to repent of, 4, but who started, he was glad to say, with a clean ; sheet. (Cheers). To Mr. Charlton Parr, their new ; Mayor, they all wished long life, they all wished for him ' that there might be a period of administration during ; his year or years of office—he hoped it would be years ' (cheers)—in which he might prove himself to be so ; strong a man that the things of the past would be ren- dered impossible in the future, and that the matters they were met to grumble about and expose would be ; things of the past, and that the wretched utterance that ; was given voice to in that meeting three weeks ago ' would never be given voice to again—that just ; as their past bad been bad so their future would be bad. Be wanted them to hold up the standard of Warrington so that public representatives must not he telling them as some had done Since he was there last—what it cost ; them. (Laughter,) What it cost them—that was the ; honour of the thing. (Cheers.) It was the highest honour that could be put on any man. He held that the ; public representative should be picked out of the crowd as the Most honest, as toe most able, and the straight- est. %Vas not that an honour that a man ought to be proud of instead of grumbling and telling them how much ' it cost? (Laughter.) It was one Of those instances he deeply deplored but it none the less showed the low con- dition of mind which many of their representatives had got into arid out of which he hoped they would very aeon be delivered. (Cheers.) Many things had happened since their last meeting. He did not dream when be was here that within a few hours, so to speak, one of the rottenest cities in the world would free itself from twenty ye ire of t cranny. ((Theers.) He did not think that New York would cast off the shackles as it had done. It stood to-day as one of tree monuments, as one of the cities that had learnt the principle and acted upon it. Warrington could imitate New York just as New York had imitated Manchester. (Laughter). Alluding to a case of municipal trading at Darwen, Mr Williams said that the gentleman implicated decided to resign his seat rather than occupy a position which might be open to misconception. That was a pattern 'for Warrington. If a man was on a company,he did not care whether it was a tile company or a slat 3 Company (laughter) or a colliery company, he must make his 'selection whether be would remain on the company or in the Council. They could not serve God and mammon and they could not be in a City Council and at the same time be a member of the board of a limited Company that was trading with the Council. That was his (the speaker's) position and the moment they left that position they got into the quick sands which landed them in no end of trouble. He had been wondering during the course of this con- troversy where the clergy and ministers of Warrington were ;it had been one of the puzzles to him. Some of them, they told him were on the other side. He could not think that. They would be a poor lot ; they would not be worth their salaries if they were on the other side. The Dissenting clergy, the Church of England clergy, the Catholic clergy, where were they in the matter ? voice: Minding their business). Some- body said they were minding their business. If the work of the ministers or the clergymen was not in the direction of pure public life, the clergymen or the ministers were net worth their salt. New he wanted their Council to be put straight. Consider what a terrible thing it was to have a Council of • thirty-six men, most of whom, or many of whom were ;weak. After hinting at an approaching further scandal in Manchester Mr Willliams went on to say that he seldom heard a more pitiable declaration than that which was made at the meeting of the Council on November 9th when the father of the Council, Alderman Sutton, said tnat notwithstanding all the hard things that had been said against the present Council, he main- tained that the town had never had a better vet of representatives that they had at present (A Voice : " Rats " and laughter). It was the finest Council in fact that ever was, added Mr Williams. The fact was that the Town Council of Warrington was what they called a mutual admiration society. (Laughter.) Artemis Ward once wrote to a man in town and asked bow the show business was going on in the town, because, he said, " I am just coming over to your town and I am going to give you an order for my II placards," He added in a postscript—and he (the speaker) thought if would suit the Warrington Town Council—" You scratch my back and I'll scratch your back." Well, they wanted to reform this body of thirty-six back-scratchers. (Laughter.) The Chairman had called attention to the fact that all these men who had gone into the Council lately had signed one of the weakest, one of the most intolerable documents be had

div.head: Mr. Norbury Williams and the Zillah Shipping and Carrying Co.: Ltd. [TO THE EDITOR OF THE EXAMINER.]
div.p: Mr. Norbury Williams and the Zillah Shipping and Carrying Co.: Ltd. [TO THE EDITOR OF THE EXAMINER.]

Sir,—l am given to understand that Mr Norbury I Williams made a statement on Thursday night to the eff set that this Company is carrying setts tor the Warrington Corporation. Will you permit me to give this an unqualified denial, for the Company has never done anything for the Cor- poration, and the only circumstance that could give rise to such a suggestion iS the following. Mr Ewart had obtainsi the coat ract for laving the train lines and long after he had got it I hays been told he learned that the setts could be brought here cheaper by water than by rail, upon Which latter he had based his con- tract. After sundry inquiriss in Liverpool he was introduced to us and we agreed with him to carry the setts by water to Widnes. Nsitber the Corporation nor the shareholders kaew anything of this arrangement with him, for the business is conducted by a managing owner and a firm of ship brokers in Liveroool. Another error Mr Williams made was in stating that Mr Couacillor lieough is the Chairman of the Company. This is not So. He is not nor has he ever been.—Yours truly. Warrineton, 22v1
G. SAVAGE, Chairman. 1901

Mr. Norbury Williams and H. Ingram, Limited.

information at the expense of the feelings of other people considerably less guilty than himself. Those of your readers who studied my first letter carefully and were present at Thursday night's meet- ing will agree that the point of that letter was thereat proved up to the hilt. At that meeting, in the coolest imaginable way, this soi-disant purity committee exe- cuted a complete change ot front. To meet the incon- venient facts with which they were confronted in the case of Mr Forshaw and others these gentlemen who, up to now, have gone in for COOMIJ4 wife campaign, and who actually summoned (and packed) last night's meting to oppose all munici- pal trading, announced at that meeting that in future , their deaunciations were to be reserved for dipeetors of Companies only. So that a member of the Corporation may hold nine-tenths of the shares of a Company trading with the Corporation but he must not be a Director. Further my poor little £5O in Ingram's was distorted and twisted into every conceivable instrument of evil, whilst the £1,300 of Mr. Forshaw was condoned and approved. Could disingenuousness fur tiler go? D 3 the people of this town really think that men who can execute such feats of moral gymnastics as these are burning with the pure fire of righteous indignation at the enormities of municipal trading as now carried on ? Let there be an inquiry by all means if that alone will stanch the present appalling otxtfl ow of malice and slander. Stopped it must be at any price if the town is to be saved from the moral degradation which must be the unfailing concomitant of an agitation characterised by so much that is untrue, uncharitable, and revolting as this.—Yours truly,

TO THE EDITOR. Sir,—Our attention has been called to a statement contained in one of Mr Norbury Williams's letters to the effect that a certain firm (referred to as "A. B. and Co.") applied to the Corporation for electric power, and that on the same day our foreman called upon A. B. and Co. and asked for the order for motors, and that we wrote to the same effect on that date. No application for power has ever been made to the Uorporattun tiy re: ann Co. Our Mr Ingram has acted as electrical adviser to A.. B. and Co. for the past twelve months, and during that time he and we have completely equipped A. B. and Co.'s works with electric fittings for the purpose of light. All that time our men have been busily employed in the works, and our Mr Ingrain has had frequent con9Ultationg with A. B. and Co.'s managing directors as to the advisability of taking power from the Corporation and the fixing of motors. During October the Corporation laid mains to A. B. and Co.'s works, and we were called upon to make the attachments for light. Our foreman, seeing that the mains provided also for power, called at A. B. and Co.'s office on the 4th inst., and asked if anything was being done about the motors, which had been the subject of such frequent discussion between A. B. and Co. and our Mr Ingram. Mr Ingrain has been ill in bed for two months past, and it was at his request and on his be- half that our foreman called at A. B.and Co.'s to inquire about the motors. At the same time Mr Ingram sent word to our clerk to make formal application for the order. No word or hint was ever given to us by any official I of the Corporation about any application being made by A. B. and Co. ; as a matter of fact, none was made. The laying of mains is usually preceded by such an application, hence our foreman's information to Mr Ingram. Bearing in mind that we have professionally advised A. B. and Co. all through their electrical developments, , we fail to see how we could be regarded as dependent in I any way on the Corporation officials for news. Indeed, it was we who informed the Corporation of A. B. and Co.'s intentions respecting motors. We never received the slightest hint from the officials of any application from A. B. and Co. (who had made none), and it is not true that our foreman made any such statement in their office as is alleged. The grounds given as causes of favour to ourselves are absurd, seeing that competitors of ours have, as shareholders, not merely aoCouncillor, but an Alderman as well.—Yours, Szc.,
F. R. ROBERTS.

div.head: Another Speech by Mr. Norbury Williams.
div.p: Another Speech by Mr. Norbury Williams.
Warrington's " Miserable and Contemptible

div.head: Condition."
div.p: Condition."

Last Friday night Mr Norbury Williams addressing a meeting in St. Peter's School, Moaton-lane, Manchester, in support of the candidature of Mr James Johnson for the representation of the Blackley and Moston Ward of the Manchester City Council,urged the electors to send Mr Johnson to the City Council because of the need there was for men of honesty and ability in the administration of local affairs. The mistake was Cu elect men simply because they were of this or that political colour. The other evening he was at the largest municipal meeting I ever held in this country. It was at Warrington-3,000 people inside and 2,030 outside. Why was this interest taken ? Why was it that the whole of Warrington was at this moment seething with excite meat on this question of municipal government ? It was because of this, that for long years the only ning asked of a man was" Are you a Red ?" or " Are you a Bluer and as a consequence the municipality or that town had been eaten to the very core by jobbery and the most horrid corruption. He did not know it there was s more corrupt or more contemptible borough, from the mnnicipal point of view in the United King- dom. He bad been in the habit of saying we were far from perfect in Manchester. So we were, but if he were a burgess of Warrington he would be ashamed to live in it if he did not raise the whole place and endea- vour to bring about a new condition of things. Why, be was almost proud of Manchester when he began to think of places like Warrington. But the good govern- ment of Manchester so far as it was good, had only been brought about by constant vigilance and work on the part of some people. The vigilance had not been half of what it ought to have been, or we should not have had these constantly recurring troubles, abuses, and scandals. He said at Warrington that Manchester was going to have another of these scandals. Personally, he was sick of these things. He did not like to be involved in them. But it was a healthy sign that they came to the surfarie, and it was because of " that wretched borough," never having brought them to the surface that it was in such a miserable and contemptible condition tc-day. Too many members of the Council were mere followersy Like ducklings in a pond, when the big bird moved the followed. In conclusion he said ,there are many thing that will have to be said, and if we are driven to it a shall state them, if nobody else does. Cheers.) They will have to be published. No Warrington business in Manchester; (Cheers.) N3hob-nobbing of Liberal. and Conservatives together in order to keep the general public outside No. no. (Cheers.)

div.p: 11. INGRAM, LIMITED.

Sir,—Since writing the above letter the meeting at she Parr Ball has been held. At that meeting Mr Nor- bury Williams, conveniently ignoring our letter, reiter- ated his charges against us, and claimed that he would prove them. We challenge him to prove (1) That A. B. and Co., made an application for electric power to the Corporation. (2) that we were informed of this by a member of the Electricity Committee or by an official ofthe Electricity Department. If Mr Williams can prove these charges we will pay £2O t 3 the Warrington Infirmary on condition that he pays a similar sum if he fails in his proof. We would suggest that he and we should each name a magistrate of the Borough and that .they should name a third to act as the umpire. If this challenge is declined the public will know what conclusion to come to. Yours truly, H. INGIUM, LIMITED.

div.head: Councillor F. R. Roberts' Final Reply to Councillor Forshaw. [TO THE EDITOR OF THE si EEALIINER."]
div.p: Councillor F. R. Roberts' Final Reply to Councillor Forshaw. [TO THE EDITOR OF THE si EEALIINER."]

Sir,--As Mr Forshaw has (whilst charging -ire with making mis-statements) admitted every charge I made against him I should not have troubled you with another letter bot foi two things which he has thought right to say. The first is that I was present when there was moved, and supported, his ridiculous resolution about the trading of members of the Council and their partnerp. The resolution was proposed and carried at a meeting of the General Purposes Com- mittee (which consists of the entire Council) in Novem- ber last. I was not present at that meeting and there- fore could neither have voted for nor otherwise supported Mr Forshaves resolotiO3. The minutes came up for confirmation at the Council meeting in Decem- ber, at which I was present, but as the Council, sitting as the General Purposes Committee, had adopted the resolution aad as the resolution was perfectly innocuous though superfluous, I did not think it worth while to raise my solitary voice against it, especially as one of my Professional brethren was concerned in it. The Council has since expunged the resolution. The second question that requires some elucidation is that of Mr Forshaw's presence at the first Parr Hall meeting. Mr Forsbaw is not quite in- genuous in his reference to thiP. He does not Say that he was never present at the meeting, but that he was not there when his name was called out. The truth is that Mr Forshaw was present at the meeting , until a minute or two before that event. Then, whilst Mr Norbury Williams was amplifying in intense enjoy- ment his announcement that he intended t) call upon the seven assenting Councillors by name Mr Forshaw was seen to depart. But neither in his letter to you nor elsewhere has Mr Forshaw denied that he did, whilst himself a share- holder to the extent of £1,300 in one limited company and of a considerable sum in another company trading with the Corporation, actually assent to the programme I of the no-trading agitators, and also tarnish them with

in politics to place before the people an aspiration to what might engage the attention of the legisla- ture were Liberals and Radicals to compose their differences and again return to power. His lordship is already a member of one of the Houses of Parliament, and has; therefore no particular axe to grind on his own account. His views of politics, so opposed to the traditions and instincts of his own rank must be the result of independent judgment and genuine altruistic feeling. His opinions on the distracting causes of trouble among politicians of his way of thinking may therefore be taken as worth noting. He takes care to place the war and the question of Imperialism in their true proportion. They I form but parts of a wide plane of observation and operation which every Liberal with the broad I sympathies of his creed ought to keep in view. It is clearly suicidal for a party with such a platform within reach to fritter away its energies in inter- neCine strife over points of view either regarding the war or Imperialism. And yet upon these two topics the noble earl has definite opinioas, reason- able and temperate, and such as his party might find no difficulty in making a basis upon which to unite for common action. He says if the term pro- Boer meant that he was against his country in this war, he was not a pro-Boer. This is a fine dis- tinction, which many Radicals are unable to draw. More's the pity. The just claims of the Boers to conside ration, even as a beaten con- quered race, must find a generous response in every true Liberal; but it does not follow that the sympathies of any party of our countrymen should go so far as to desire the continuance of the deadly and demoralising struggle still going on in South Africa, much less Success to those who are still in arms against us. It may be safely con jectured that in no other country in the world, professing civilisation, would there have been witnessed or tolerated so much adverse feeling towards the success of the nation's arms. It is quite true as the EARL of 13 UCKINGHAMSRIRE has said,the term pro-Boer has been so shamefully misused and distorted by the I Tories that nobody knew the meaning of it at all. The Tories had a p arty object in view in demolish- ing the fine distinction to which we have alluded; but there is the aore necessity for Liberals—and Radicals, too—to insist on the distinction being drawn which shall make the stigma of being un— patriotic impossible of application. In the same sensible way his lordship deals with Imperialism. The term Liberal Imperialist is an unfortunate one, chiefly because it has been covered with unde- served opprobrium and reproach by both parties. But, as the noble EARL says, it conveys the right thing. The Imperialist Liberal—a term which had also been much abused—should be one who is entirely and absolutely against foreign aggression and any unnecessary expansion of Empire, but who is determined to maintain and develop and I consolidate to the utmost those lands in all parts I of the world to which an Englishman is heir. When the dust of the present conflict has sub- sided, it may well be that do difficulty will be found in consolidating a Liberal party with its due proportion of Radicals on such a basis.

THE new Education The New Education Bill which the Govern- Bill. merit are likely to bring before the next session of Parliament is discussed by Dr Mlasamana, M.P., in the Fortnightly .Re" view. From indications that have been given by Ministers, it is evident that what the Government

intend to do is to ask the municipalities each to ' electlan Education Committee, to deal in the first , instance with secondary education, and in the next with the elementary work of the School Bards, which it is intended ultimately to super- sede. Dr MACNAMARA throws a very clear light en the motives for the Government's action. Ere says the Governarent do not like the School Boards; being eluted exclusively for education they do their work more energetically than the , Government desire. This may be confirmed by re- ferences to the subject which memeers of the Government have dropped here and there in nio" meats of confidence. The hon. member quotes all excellent example. At Bristol Sin JOHN GODS I told an audience with amazing frankness what is : ' really the key to Tory policy in this matter of edit- ' cation.He said the members of the Government are . selected from a class that is not entirely concerned ' with the necessity or desirability of higher educr bon for the people. They hold, he says, the °pia' , ion that there are certain functions which have to : be performed in the modern life of civilised coin' , munities which are much better performed hY people who are ignorant. A lovely gospel thll,, for the new century! We have heard of tha maxim, now happily exploded, that "ignorance 10 the mother of devotion," but now we are to have the masses of the people kept in ignorance for no other reason than that they may become patient beasts of burden, and remain comfortable aht,l contented while they are exploited for the advar tage of their educated superiors. Therefore, thie , Government, who will not hear of the municipa,l; isation of gas and water, will municipalise popill° • ,education, in the hope thaa under the pressure cd ' rates, rising for all kinds of municipal measurea public interest in the cause of education 1101 gradually fade, and perhaps disappear. A more daring anachronism has never been perpetrated .: even by this retrograde Government. It will n't4 be surprising if it should lead, even more than the mismanaged, bungled war to the undoing of RS ' authors. But Dr. MACNAMARA, as a londoo , member, is specially concerned in the arrange' ments which are likely to be made for the metro' polis, with its charge of considerably more thss ' half a million scholars. The case for London le very strong. Supposing that the present Eduov, tion Committee of the County Council shoula become the authority for education, that corntolfr 1 tee has already in hand as much as it can Of through effectively in developing scientific, artistic, and technological work, besides the question commercial education, which it is now taking 11PI, and an excellent system of scholarships which ie administers. Add to this the entire element work of the London School Board, and the committee will be overwhelmed, and becola° practically useless for good work. If, on the other hand, each of the borough councils which make up the local government of the metropolis is asked to appoint a separate committee, then .: will follow divided interests, with their crop of 1 jealousies and strife, divided management, with enormously increased expense, and divided rates in the different _districts, which may vary frof

He was to announce that the collections taken in various places of worship in the town and on behalf of the Warrington Infirmary and pensary were £6O in excess of those of the 13'; vious year. An exception too, would surely have to be made when the beneficiary was blind, and derived his living from this source. The State does far too little for the afflicted, and it is one of the disgraces of the country that people have to make an exhibition of hideous injuries in order to win sympathy of a practical kind. But the able-bodied persons who choose to go about seeking to keep the traditions of the troubadour, With none of his qualities, need repressing. The bold bad cornet-player is particularly objection- able. The nigger troupes are an insult to coons. The worst profanity is the financial use of religious hymns by bleary vocalists, who have long since given themselves over to quite other thoughts. Then there are the seaside singers and the banjo- players. Their continuance is a proof that they meet a demand, otherwise the supply would not remain; but a tax would tend to make them, if one may put the matter mildly, a little more exclusive.

-- The two great Cycle shows of the year fail to disclose any novelty of a remarkable character. Last year's shows were identified with a great dis- play of the free wheel. That invention is still With us, and ,has, indeed, gained so much public favour that whether at the Crystal Palace or at the Agricultural Hall at least SO per cent of the exhibits are fitted up in this manner. This year there is nothing of importance which is really fresh. There is shown at the Crystal Palace, it is true, a cycle fitted with a sort of windmill wheel arrangement below the handle-bars, which is said to communicate extra power to the driving-wheel; but as this additional force must necessarily be derived from the resistance the revolving fan offers to the air, we admit it seems to us that what is gained in one way must be lost, and something more, in the other. In the absence of anything more sensa- tional, the feature of the shows seems to be .the advance of the motor cycle. These machines pre- sent now a great improvement on the models offered to the public only a year or two back; and, What is almost as important, the improvement is accompanied by a distinct lowering of price. The motor cycle is not, perhaps, for the young and athletic, to whom cycling is a mode of exercise and athletics rather than a mode of getting rapidly from one place to another. It presents, however, great advantages to many in its con- venience, its speed, and its radius of action—to borrow a term from naval tactics. Now that motor cycles have been proved reliable for at least a journey of one hundred and fifty miles without unreasonable stoppages, they may be expected in ever-increasing numbers both on our town and our country roads.

There was very little that was new either in the way of facts or fancies adduced at the meeting in Warrington last week on the municipal trading question. For the most part the audience had to be satisfied with the:same dish hashed up again,instead of the something they expected which would - tickle the palate. Two things were new, however. One was the question printed on a handbill, ask- ing if Mr. Parr, the present Mayor, was a share- holder in Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, Ltd., and - if that firm traded with the Corporation to the extent of £5,000 or thereabouts. Out of this question rose the second new feature, which ° was nothing less than a striking change of front on the part of the agitators. - All along they have ostensibly fought for t the principle of absolute immaculateness in Corporation trading. Every member was to Ise like Csar's wife, "above suspicion" and was not to be connected in any shape or form, even , through relations, with companies trading with the Corporation. It was a beautiful aspiration, charmingly simple—but utterly impracticable. Now that the war has been taken into their own camp, the enemy-4f we may term them such— have altered their attitude very materially. The answer to the question concerning Mr Parr— against whom nothing in the slightest degree dis- paraging is suggested—is to the effect that as he , only holds a two-thousandth part of the Pearson and 'Knowles share capital his case is one not worth serious consideration. It is not. But does L' this alter the fact that his position in the matter • 11,i contrary to the demands originally made by Mr '-'odds and his confreres on a question of principle? A ccording to this latest version of what is per- taissible in municipal trading, the whole thing l'esolves itself into a question of the degree or ex- tent to which a member of the Corporation is concerned in the management of a company. con- tracting with the Corporation. Where then is the , ,nne to be drawn? If the position of the ex-Mayor opento condemnation, on grounds of propriety, then that of the present Mayor is also. The sum total of personal interest is outside the question - •of right or wrong altogether, and in this matter Mr. Dodds and his friends stand convicted of in- consistency and bad logic. Mr. Norbury Williams only made this point, and that of the unfair methods through which the agitation is worked, clearer by the unctuous satisfaction with which he (lragged in H. Ingram Limited, and the Zillah Shipping Co. Ltd. The representation on, and trading of the former with, the Corporation, is about on a par, so far as the extent is concerned, ith the case of Mr. Parr, and Pearson and !ti.owles Limited, while in the case of the Zillah lo liipping Company. there is even less justification his remarks, as the company has never traded et iith the Corporation at all. If these matters are threfuliy considered by the ratepayers we think Will not be long in arriving at a conclusion at hs the agitation is as spurious in many respects ot:_nre leaders of it are inconsistent and biassed in Other S.

A Provincial Letter.

"Fires >, . a --- standing la'4 "11 "More Great Fires" appear as offices at theeacnines in certain of the newspaper some places present period of the year, and in unatile to co e inhabitants have found themselves of a s Pe With the mischief wrought by reason ' carcity of water. Notwithstanding the heavy downpour of rain a little more than a fortnight .e,in Ce a state of drought continues in many parts of the provinces. For instance, in a small town near Bath the other day a gentleman's mansion, with its Valuable contents, was burnt to the ground while members of several fire brigades looked on in a state of utter helplessness, through the failure of the local water supply. How many other places might find themselves in a similar predicament in the event of a sudden outbreak it is for the local auth- orities everywhere to duly consider. Another evil , state of things peculiar to the season is revealed in the almost daily:reports of lamp accidents,chiefly,of Course, in the humbler class of cottage dwellings. . Loss of lifetalmost invariably attends the upsetting ' Or explosion of these petroleum lamps,while rarely . does it happen that one or more persons are not , . seriously injured, and other damage is done. These accidents should have the effect of bringing into view the dangers associated with such lamps when theyl, are defectively constructed or improperly handled by persons not sufficiently informed as to the risks they incur. Coroners' juries do what they atl, after ascertaining the cause of deaths which l_ ave been thus brought about, to impress upon all users of oil lamps the fact that there are certain o‘nditions of safety which,if overloOked or neglect- may lead to the most disastrous consequences ; but yet the evil goes on.

--- In view of the recommendation of the Select Committea on Fire Brigades to discontinue the Sending of fire engines out of the towns, owing to the defenceless state in which the latter may some- times find themselves, the lot of rural districts in CBB of fire is not a happy one. The committee, too :mere inclined to minimise the efficiency tf volun- teer fire brigades,believing that the principle of en- rthe performance of a public duty to private private4.4d irresponsible persons is an unsound one nd that it has hitherto given very unsatisfactory lesulte, This may be very true, but it seems also ver.v lame and halting. That great philosopher of -;1r8 Mr John Morley, some time ago taught us that e could not have the best we should endeavour th content ourselves with and make the best use of e Second best. Possibly the committee did ot think of this.

Provincial payers of the Income Tax whose in— come hasjor some years been small enough to drop through the meshes of the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer's net may possible begin to quiver if what has recently been reported as to Sir Michael Hicks- Beach's intentions should prove true. It has more than once been pointed out in certain newspapers that Sir William Harcourt let off prematurely and unnecessarily those incomes within a hundred and fifty pounds a year, and that the abatement up to seven hundred pounds was a financial mistake. And new the " economist " comes to ithe conclusion that the abatement made at the lower end of the scale of income has been carried to excess. Incomes under £l6O go free, and those of £4OO are entitled to an abatement of £l6O, the abatement gradually diminishing up to £7OO, on which sum the abate- ment is seventy pounds. From a Parliamentary return, just issued, it appears that of 752,296 per- sons individually assessed, as many as 723,376 had 'incomes under .£7OO, and were entitled to abate- ment. Omitting the odd figures, the amount of the incomes of these was 189 million pounds. The income of the fifty-eight thousand ;firms assessed amounted to nearly eighty-five millions. Twenty- five thousand public companies were assessed, and the amount of income assessable was 193 millions. The income derived from 8,432 municipal corpora- tions represented about eleven millions. If the Chancellor of the Exchequer looks to the income tax for increasing the revenue he will have before him the official return from which these figures are taken, and it may, perhaps,lead him to pause before making any considerable additien to this tax.

Representative bodies in many parts of the pro- vinces are giving special attention to the treat- ment of Consumptive Patients; and side by side with this movement, there is much discussion as to the best means ofpreventing consumption. The causes of the disease are being inquired into, and also its increasingly fatal consequences; and ques- tions are asked whether the ordinary and average dwelling-house is what it should be, and in how many rooms, even of the wealthy classes, there is efficient ventilation. The average dining.room is practically a closed box, in which the air is ren- dered foul by the breath of the occupants, and the fumes from oil or gas lights. Let anyone who wishes to test the air in his lighted room mount a pair of steps and place his head near the ceiling. A correspondent suggests that the sanitary authori- ties should compel builders to ventilate the living rooms, just as they require efficient drainage; lack of ventilation, or the deprivation of fresh air, being one of the great causes of consumption. The correspondent condemns underground kitchens, and draws attention to the absence in most houses of proper appliances .for ensuring personal cleanliness. It is generally recog- nised that disease and dirt go together, and that foul hot-air in dwelling-houses or factories is so much poison, inducing consumption; yet, how little is done to deal effectually with these evils in the construction of the modern dwelling-Place ! If more were thought of and done in this direction, the less need there would be for consumption hospitals and all their attendant expense and troubles. But as matters stand,let it be adcled,these hospitals are absolutely essential, and should be liberally supported.

"On American lines," is a phrase as commonly met with in English newspapers now as were the words, "They manage these things better in France,";until the time of " afairelDreyfus." But there can be nothing less captivating from the ordinary Englishman's point of view, in one phrase than the other if the news be true that an influ- ential American syndicate are about to erect an office building, on American lines, in the heart of London. It will be enough to make many people wish that 'Columbus had never been so fortunate. The only jot of consolation derivable from the announcement is that the proposed building will be in London, and not in the provinces. For it is, in- deed, to be a sky-scraper, and will tend to suggest that the only way to accommodate the swarming millions of the world's greatest capital, is by either soaring,above or going below. In the Strand,ani ten storeys high, it may be deemed. beautiful, but the appearance of New York buildings, of a similar character has not struck the fancy of many English- men who have seen them in that light. An idea of the sizels gathered from the fact that the structure will have an area of one hundred and twenty-five thousand square feet. It is well for the people in the neighbourhood,that the Strand is at its broadest where the proposed edifice is to be erected ; but if as reported this is but the pioneer of others, and the adjacent narrow streets are to give place to similar monster sites, London's great centre will be a place of hideous depression such as may the provinces never have to witness!

Temperance Sunday is variously observed in London and the provinces, and again, probably, as between one portion of the latter and another. That is to say, temperance sermons are preached and Sunday School addresses on temperance are delivered on an early Sunday in November in London, and on another Sunday later on in the month in the provinces, while in one provincial district the day set apart as Temperance Sunday is not the one observed as such in another district Sunday last in Devon and Cornwall was Temper • ance Sunday. Why should there be this absence of uniformity ?

div.head: WARRINGTON CHURCH SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON CHURCH SOCIETY.
Lecture on John Wesley.

-- Under the auspices of the Warrington Church Society, a lecture was delivered in the Co-operative Hall on Wed- nesday evening by the Rev. A. S. Cameron, who took for his subject John Wesley and the Evangelical revival." There was a large attendance, Mr. Charles White presiding. The LECTUREE dealt with his subject in an able and interesting manner. He pointed out that at the time when the Methodist movement commenced the Church was apathetic, lifeless and inert, and the teaching was latitudinarianism, which was aimed at the intellect alone. The Methodists revived a personal religion. The history of the movement was reviewed, and in deal- ing with Wesley's Churchmanship the lecturer quoted bis -words " I live and die a member of the Church of England and no one who regards my advice will ever separate from it." At another time Wesley said "Be ye Church of England men still" and in speaking of the Holy Communion he said " Let anyone who has any desire to please Gad or love for his own soul communi- cate as often as he can." His actions, however, did not square with his words, and by his actions lee made a separation from the Church inevitable. Be ordained priests and deacons and went through the form of consecrating bishops and per- suaded himself that to set up a rival ministry to the church was not separation. Directly Wesley's direct inflaanca was removed his followers thought it ut and separated. They were right in blaming the hurch for not being able to ret Lin the enthusiastic Methodists within her own bounds. They might blame the church for the eh of schism. Whatever the in- fluence of schism might be, they could at least pray for unity and remember that jute- as it Was bitterness and hostility on the part of Churchmen which was partly respensible far the Methodist schism that when they came back again it must be through their (the Church people's) love and kindness. Wesley stool out as the greatest religious figure In the 18th century and to him was due the revival of personal religion in England. The lecturer pointed out that many of the Methodists remained in the church and formed the Evangelical party, who like Wesley taught a personal religion—a religion of the heart. It remained for the next century to teach that religion was not concerned with the intel- lect alone, or with the heart alone,but that it was meant to include the whole of man and that his body, soul and spirit must be brought into his worship. There must be a stately ritual to impress the eye, the best of music and art, and at least seen reverence of body to Christ in His courts as they would pay to an earthly monarch in his courts. The lecturer conclude.' by saying that the great lesson which the Methodists taught was the union of the soul with God. (Applause). The lecture was illustrated with limelight views, Mr H N Houghton manipulating the lantern. Dr. GUEST Gonliar.i, proposed a vote of thanks to the lecturer, and said he had always been intimately acquainted with Methodism, and telt a great interes and sympathy with the Methodists. He believed theret was among Methodists a considerable force of opinion that would ultimately lead to a great many of there returning to their mother church, the Church of England. (Applause). The Rev. F. E. POWELL seconded, and the motion was carried with acclamation.
