div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARPI
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARPI
ELECTION.
Result of the Poll.

The later stages-of the School Board Election,like the former, have been full of the most intense interest. Wednesday, the polling day, was a most fitting climax to a contest which has been essen- tially one of the most exceptional in the annals of local electioneering. It has been more than inter- esting; it has been unique. The Progressive party, Messrs W Handley, F J Norman, Pritchard,Posnett, and S Taylor,were the first in the field by some two weeks, and this gave them a decided advantage. This activity was, however, more than counterbalanced by the voluminous amount of literature, dealing more with the local financial aspect of the question than the broader educational issues at stake published by the other side. The Rev R H Stables was the general secretary,or to be truer, the commander-in-dhief of the voluntary party con- sisting of Canon Wood, Messrs E Imison, J Littler, and W J Cunningham. Father Chambers repro-, sented the Catholic interest. As at the previous election three years ago the rallying cries of the Clerical party were " Down with the rates" and "the best education with efficiency and economy." To this the Progressives replied with the trite sen- tence "Truth, justice and an equal chance for every child," Perhaps the slums of Runcorn have never been so well visited as they have been during the last fortnight. On both sides there has been an army of canvassers in which the ladies of the town have played by no means an unimportant part. On both sides they stood shoulder to shoulder with their brothers and had it not been for their heroic exertions the organizations of the two parties could never have coped with the electorate. So keen have been the respective canvasaers,that the voters during the last few days were wearied of their assiduous attentions and it has been stated that many abstained from voting owing to the con- tinued pressure exerted first by one set of can- vassers and then the other. The printers, too, have had an exceptionally busy time of it. Hand bills by the score each with some new argument, cunningly put, have been published from the com- mittee rooms of the opponents and the entire col- lection forms an interesting and even somewhat instructive anthology of local educational literature No sooner has some new vein of thought been struck by one side and made to glisten before the eyes of the ratepayer than the reply has been speedily forthcoming which has dulled the sparkle of wit or damaged the value of the argu- ment. The town literally has been flooded with ihandbills and; between the bable of conflicting opinions and the repeated calls of the canvasser it is little wonder that the already per- plexed elector has been well-nigh distracted. Old Runcorn inhabitants assert that there has never been an election fought with such vigour and tenacity and that there has been far more interest displayed than in any previous election whether Parliamentary or Municipal. The outcome of the paper warfare was an interesting " open letter" correspondence between Canon Wood and Mr F J Norman printed in handbill fashion and circulated very largely in the town. The matter dealt with was the cost of the transfer of the Wesleyan Schools to the Board but as our readers doubt- less know all about the subject we will not weary them with restating the arguments pro and con. Probably the last has not been heard of the matter. The statements of both parties as to' what is truth," are so conflicting and the issues being so important that it is absolutely necessary, if our public men are entitled to the re- spect which they ought to command, that the truth of certain allegations should be ascertained without further delay regardless of expense. There were four polling booths situated at the Board Schools, Victoria-road,for Newtown and Heath Wards the Church Schools, Central and Bridgewater; Mill Brow School, Halton Ward, and Trinity Schools. Mersey Ward. Fortunately the day was all that could

be desired, With the exception of a slight shower in the afternoon everything was favour- able for a heavy poll, and as a matter of fact it is the heaviest that has, perhaps, ever taken place. Had the election day been on :the Saturday instead of the Wednesday, there is no doubt the poll, large though it was, would have been considerably augmented owing to the watermen being enabled to vote. At an early hour the workers were sent out to " compel the wanderers to come in outlof the byways"to record their votes and by 9.30 a very fair number had been recorded Polling was slack every where in the morning and alter- uoon bat from 12 be 1 noon and after 5.30 there was a steady stream of electors which kept everyone con- cerned at high pressure. Al! day there was a very large concoursa of people outside the various committee rooms but towards 7 p.m. at all the booths there were dense masses of people who occa- sionally cheered their respective partizans. Traps, carriages, were all requisitioned to fetch up the laggard voter and to wards the close one or two exciting incidents were witnessed. To the credit of both parties, keen and bitter though the contest has been, there was an utter absence of anything approach- ing ill humour or friction. Both sets of workers regarded each other as honourable opponents and absolutely nothing of a rowdy character or unpleasant nature oc- curred during the whole of the day. So well, indeed, was order maintained that the police had actually reason to complain that there was nothing for them to do. At 8 p.ra.the poll was declared duly chsed in all the wards, the ballot boxes being afterwards cmveyed to the , Town Hall where they were counted on Thursday morning. Following the poll on Wednesday the Pro- 1 gressives held an enthusiastic meeting at Brunswick School and the Voluntaryists also held a similar meet- ing at their Cmunittee Room. The result of the election was announced about 3.30 on Thursday afternoon. The reason that the rounters were so long in coming to a decision was owing to a recount being necessary to determine the correctness of the nuthbers polled for Messrs Posnett and Unison. The following was the result : F J Norman, 3079 Canon Wood, Father Chambers, W Handley, J Pritchard, S Taylor, J Littler, E Imison, R Posnett,
W Cunnitigh!tm,

Last year the figures were : Chambers, 1990 ; Cunningham, 2548 ; Handley, 1813 ; Imison, 2510 ; Littler, 2304 ; Norman, 2022 •, \Yukon, 1756 ; Pritchard, 1941 ; Taylor, 1855 ; Wood, 2661 ; Col ier. 667 ; It will thus be seen that the Clerical party polled 53 votes less than last year, while the Progressives rolled 3,007 more irrespective of the votes given to Mr W Collier. There was a great crowd waiting outside the Town Hall steps to learn the result,and the voting came as • great surprise to everyone. Everyone seemed sorry that Mr Cunningham had lost his seat. and one of the church candidates aptly remarked on hearing the news that he was the last man he would have thought to have been unseated. Thus ends one of the most exciting elections ever fought in Runcorn.

div.head: Meeting in Support of the Church
div.p: Meeting in Support of the Church
Candidates.

On Thursday at the Mariners Mission a meeting was held in support of the Church Candidates. Mr J Meadowcreft presided and delivered a lengthy speech. The meeting was also addressed by the candidates and Mr J Johnson MEETING AT ET. EDWARD'S. A further meeting in support of the candidature of the Church party was held on Friday under the presi- dency of Father Chambers, The candidates addressed the meetiag at length, There was a fair attendance.

. , FINAL MEETING IN SUPPORT OF TETE CLERICAL PARTY. On Monday, at the National Schools, the final meeting was held, Mr W Timmins in the chair. There was a good audience. Speeches were delivered by all the candidates.

IdEETING IN SUPPORT OF THE PROGRESSIVE CANDIDATES. On Monday evening a public meeting in support of the five Progressive candidates was held in the Bruns- wick Schools. There was a large attendance. Mr A R Norman presided, and there were on the platform the Rev J Hirst Hollowell, Rev A. Wells, Rev J Osborne ; Messrs S Taylor, F J Norman, James Pritchard, R El Posnett, W Handley, 8 C Bickett, J R Frith, J Wilson and others. The Chairman said that one thing which was made much of by the other side was " the godless education of the Board School." (14 Shame.") He could give a ' reference to a Board School at Wavertree to the effect that a hymn was sung and prayer nsade, and the prayer thus taught was afterwards said by the children at their mother's knee. They had boys present from the Runcorn Board School, and he would ask them to step on the platform and repeat the formula taught, so that even f ratepayer could see for himself the religious Instruction that was given. (Applause.) The boys then,amidst a burst of applause, trooped on the platform, and sang in excellent style the stirring hymn entitled "Fight the good fight." They after wards went through the religious formula of the Board Scho)l, closing with the Lord's Prayer. The Chairman, continuing, said that was the kind of thing which was termed godless education. After that formula was gone through by the scholars a biblica- reading was given, special attention being given to biol.

graphy and the life of the Lord Jesus Christ, and His parables, Mr Frith moved, and Mr Wilson seconded the follow- ing resolution, which was unanimously carried : "That this meeting pledges itself by every effort to secure the election of Messrs Handley, Norman, Posnett, Pritchard, and Taylor at the election on Wednesday next."

The Rev J. Hirst Hollowell spoke at length and criti- cised severely the speeches of the clerical candidates. Mr Taylor said he was prepared to stand by his chal- lenge in spite of what had been said by the other side. Mr Posnett said that those who wished to touch the educational heritage of their children should be told to keep their' hands off." Mr F J Norman, in the course of a strong speech, read a letter he had sent to Canon Wood. Votes of thanks terminated the meeting.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT],

As I predicted last week, the progressives have won by a handsome majority. Though Mr Posnett has only just beaten Mr Cunningham the totals show that the Clerical party have been thoroughly discomfited and smitten hip and thigh. Mr Norman heads the list with over 3,000 votes and this will be a source of satisfaction to all:educationalists. He fully deseives this high honour and even his opponents will admit that his position has been justly earned. Doubtless the victory is due to the superior organi- zation of the Progressives and the number of willing workers ready to wipe off the stigma of three years ago. Compared with the last election the Progressives were considerably more alert and keen. They were in the field first and this always counts for a good deal. The " ratepayers " candi- dates have received a very rude shock and it will take them a long long time to reduce the majority against them. It may safely be asserted that the rates will not go up in consequence of the change, but that, if possible,the reverse will be the case. At all events" the most efficient -education " will be given " with the strictest economy."

7,While jubilant at the result of the poll,sympathy must be tendered to the retiring member. Mr Cunningham has worked well and served the rate- payers faithfully. Still it is the " fortune of war " as a Frenchman would say,and one ought to be able to preserve a steady equilibrium,when encountering either success or failure. Probably in another sphere of labour to which Mr Cunningham is de- voted, his spare time will be more than fully occu- pied and while his departure is to be regretted it was none the less necessary that one of the Volun- taryists should ba "non suited." Hearty good wishes to the new Board.

div.p: Frodsham Petty Sessions.

WEDNESDAT.—Before Mr Q •Crossland:Taylor (in the chair) ant Mr John Murray. THEFT Hy A Woman'. —Ellen Smith, alias Cheatham. was charged with stealing 55 In cash from Samuel Worrell, of Church-street,Prodsharn, on Saturday night. The prosecutor stated that about 7.30 on Saturday night he was standing in Ship-street when prisoner came to hint and asked if he had got anything in his pocket. Witness replied that he had a copper or two, and prisoner asked him for a halfpenny to buy some onions. He gave her a halfpenny, and prisoner came nearer to him and put her hand into his pocket. She then went away, and he missed two half-crowns from his pocket. He saw the prisoner shortly afterwards and asked her for the two half-crowns but she simply used bad language and he detained her until a police constable came on the scene. Prisoner was then given into custody. Evidence was given to show that prisoner changed two half-crowns and a 24 piece in Frocisham the same evening. When searched at the Police Station 5s was found in her possession. consisting of a 2s piece. live six- pences, and sixpence in copper. The prisoner said the prosecutor gave her the two half-crowns and some coppers. She was sent to gaol for 14 days' hard labour. div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
Railway Fatality at Ditton Junction.

On Thursday morning a woman named Ellen Stanton,4o, met with a shocking death whilst cross- ing the line at Ditton Junction. She was engaged cleaning waiting looms and was carrying a bucket of water when she was cut to pieces by an express I train. The unfortunate woman lived with her blind husband in Wood's Cottage, Ditton. Ship Canal Pollution—Action Against the Salford Corporation?

The Mersey and Irwell Joint Committee are bringing an action against the Salford Corporation for the alleged pollution of the Manchester Ship Canal. The proceedings are being taken in the Salford County Court. and the case will come before Judge Parry on the 16th of December. The Ear and Hearing. This was the subject of Professor Stirling's I lecture in the Co-operative Hall, on Tuesday even- ing. The task of making an audience understand the phenomena of sound and the way one appreci- ates sound, he saiJ, was a somewhat more difficult task than that of leading them to understand and appreciate light. That was due in part to the immense complexity of the apparatus in man by which sounds were interpreted. The lecturer pro- ceeded to show that a sounding body was a vibrat- ing body, and referred to the three distinct features of sound—pitch, strength or amplitude and the quality of sounds. Proceeding to describe the apparatus of bearing, which consists of the outer, middle and inner ear, the lecturer incidentally gave some valuable information regarding common affections of the ear. Sound, he said, impinged upon the membrane or drum of the ear after passing through the outer ear In referring to the secretion of wax in the ear he said the wax was very bitter to the taste and served as a barrier against the entrance of small insects into the ear. Some people suffered from a consider- able quantity of wax in the ear, and the lecturer stated that the best way to clear the ear was by the use of a syringe and soapwater. Those who used the. edge of a towel or some such means to remove it pushed the wax on the drum of the ear, where it hardened and prevented the membrane from vibrating to sound. The lecturer described how sound is conveyed through the ear to .the brain, and afterwards described how,upon a similar principle, it has been made possible to reproduce sound by means of a phonograph or gramaphone. Some interesting views were thrown on the screen, dahowing the auricle in man in animals, _the lecturer pointing out the similarity n several in- tances. An interesting lecture concluded with a emonstration on the gramaphone.

At Weston Point, en Monday, an inquest was held Loaching the death of Joseph Barnes, aged six months, son of George Barnes, Lnnt's-row, Weston Point, who died from the result of burns on the Sunday.—The evidence showed that on Friday night the child was dressed in a flannelette night- gown and put by the fire tied in a chair. The usual meeting of the above was held on Satur- day evening in the Greenway-road School. The President (Mr Thomas Heesom) occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance of officers and members. At the close of the business Mr Daniel, Bisbrown read a paper entitled " The Rev Charles Garrett: an appreciation." The writer said that Mr Garrett was born in Shaftesbury in the year 1823. He was converted when 15 years of age and identified himself with the Methodist Church, Shortly after this he signed the temperance pledge; after bearing a lecture by Mr John Cassell, who afterwards became the bead of the great publishing firm. Mr Garrett became corresponding secretary of the Anti-corn Law League, and he was brought in contact with John Bright and Richard Cobden, and other lea lers of the movement. As a speaker he was a warm supporter of the social questions of the day—especially the temper- ance cause. In 1852 he was accepted for the Wesleyan ministry, and spent three years at Rich- mond College. He travelled in many circuits and soon occupied front rank as a preacher. He was a great moral force in the country. Ile took an active part to relieve distress during the cotton famine, when the closing of the Lancashire mills placed half-a-million of operators dependent on charity. The writer referred to his mission work in Manchester and Liverpool, and his appointment as president of the Wesleyan Conference. In con- clusion the writer spoke of his intense earnestness and enthusiasm in temperance reform. His con- stancy was to be admired. "He stood four Near@ before every wind that blew." He was in fact, an example worthy of imitation. After the address there was a discussion in whizh the following officers and members took part :—Messrs Samuel Tomlinson, Alfred Noden, Thomas Clarke, Thomas R Whyte, Thomas Beeson', and Joseph Astbury (Halton), Mr Thomas Cooke moved a vote of thanks to Mr Bisbrown,which was seconded by Mr Edward Key, jun., and carried unanimously. THEFT BY A YOUNG MAN. At the Runcorn Police Court on Monday before Messrs F J Norman (in the chair), and E Imison, a young man named Alfred Stenzhorn was charged with stealing a sovereign belonging to John Hutchins on the 15th November.—Prosecuto ,r mate of the schooner" James and Agnes," said that on the date named his vessel was at the Runcorn Docks and his waistcoat which contained the sovereign was in the master's cabin. Prisoner was cook of the ship and belonged to London.—Prisoner was apprehended by Sergeant Gregory at the Free Library and when charged replied that he had spent the money. lie was the most hard faced young man Sergeant Gregory had ever met with. Prisoner was committed to gaol for 14 days ha rd labour.

RUGBY FOOTBALL.
By " Ovalist."

Warrington ought to have had two points out of Saturday's match with Halifax—or at any rate one point—instead of coming away defeated as they did. The home team possessed a very pr record in the League, and had only one win to their credit out of eight games, so that Warrington stood more than a fair chance of success when they set out, even though Fish was an absentee. Luck was once more against them, however, and as at Broughton they lost the game in the last five minutes of play. It all happened this way.

Very soon after the commencement of hostilities it was clear that Warrington were the superior team in. combination and smartness. Halifax only paid a brief visit to the Warrington end and then found all their ' work cut out to prevent the Warrington backs crossing the line after speedy passing runs. Harris twice looked a probable scorer, but he somehow failed at the critica inomentl generally because the full back was in the way. Warrington were very quick behind but they lacked "those finishing touches so essential to success' as a brother scribe often says on such occasions. The combination between halves and centres was excellent,' but the wings were unable to get through. Up to half time Warrington had had considerably the most of the play, but there was no score.

On resuming the Halifax men carried all before them and by sheer dash they forced their way to the War- rington line. The forwards heeled out and Riley, a strongly-built half-back, forced himself over the line, Little adding a goal. This was the spur Warrington needed. The primrose and blue was soon in the van again. Warrington got down to the other end and in almost as little time as it takes to tell Isherwood scored from a quick pass from Allen. It was a certainty either for himself or Hockenhall. Hallam took the all- important goal-kick and to the joy of his club-mates he equalised.

I certainly thought Warrington safe after this, even though Halifax were still going strongly. They did not strike one as being a scoring team and by the ordinary methods would never have got through the Warrington defence. But they were not content with ordinary methods. The forwards took the game into their own hands—or feet—and by clever wheeling and dribbling they continued to get the best of the play. Warring- ton made many an incursion into Halifax territory, but a free-kick nearly always drove them hack, the referee's conduct being particularly annoying and inexplicable. Time passed excitingly and only five minutes remained when the ball was rushed over the Warrington line and finally flew among the spectators. The referee awarded Halifax a try and the yell of delight travelled far and wide. Warrington made one desperate effort and then expired, the score reading 8 points to 5 points against them.
strike

In the dressing-room the comments on the result and the referee were sulphurous. Mr. Renton was not the appointed official and with Mr. J. Smith officiating it was generally thought Warrington would have won. Certainly the Hunslet man seemed very rough on War- rington and allowed a try at the end which not a single Halifax man appealed for. The Warrington men assert that the ball was in the air all the time and was never actually touched down by the scorer, and from what I could see of the incident it certainly seemed as if this was the case. Anyhow it was a stroke of luck for Halifax to win on Saturday and one could not blame the Warrington men for the defeat. They had played a good game.

Here is what the " Yorkshire Post " says of the match. "Once more the team from over the border dis- played superior work behind the pack, Burgess, Allen, Isherwood,and Harris playing splendidly. The Halifax forwards,however,frequently more than counterbalanced this,Kitson, Jack Riley, Bartle, and Morton each playing a lusty and sound game, whilst the front rank generally made innumerable openings,which might have increased the score. Little,as is always the case played wonderfully well, and Warrington would possibly have won had Halifax been without him. There is no doubt that the Lancastrians played the more attractive foot- ball, and the verdict for most of the game was very much in their favour. Indeed, Halifax outstayed the opposition in the latter stages, and won on the post as it were, whilst mostly having the worst of the con- test."

The "Leeds and Yorks Mercury" comments as follows .—" Though Halifax won, generally speaking they were lucky to be in that position at the finish. There was no mistaking the superiority of the iosers in the back division. Burgess continually opened out the game for the expert passing movements of llockenhall, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Harris, the last two of whom were brilliant. Hallam, too, at full back was reliable. The saviour of the Halifax men was Little, whose play was full of resource. Nicholl and Arnold, the Halifax wings, had not much chance to shine, because passing movements were generally nipped in the bud before the leather reached them. Jack Riley, Kitson, and Langliorn were the pick of the Halifax for wards,both setsjof which vrerefairly evenly matched. "

These are fair and candid expressions of opin3on from the other side, which acquit Warrington of blame for losing the match. With Fish on Jam convinced we should have won easily, the rest of the backs com- bined so well. Hockenhall did not play a good game. while Harris should have been more successful. The centres were the best pair, though Burgess and Allen worked hard. The former stuck to the ball rather too long when running across, and occasionally spoiled a good opening. Forward there was some excellent play between evenly-balanced eights,the Halifax men being , a trifle the smarter alround.

At full back, Hallam played well but was quite over shadowed by the home custodian Little, whom I saw for the first time and was much impressed with. On Saturday's form he can have very few superiors any- where, and seems just such another as Baty at his best. Safe catching, strong running and tackling, with a mighty punch make him an important factor in a game. He did more to prevent Warrington winning than even the referee which is saying a lot. There seemed no getting back after one of his tremendous punts. No wonder Little is the idol of the Halifax crowd, though his name belies him. There was no fog in Halifax during the match, and altogether the conditions were most pleasant. Travelling too was excellent, the distance between Manchester and Halifax being covered both ways in less than an ' hour.

I see that York and Holbeck, who are both in the running for the Yorkshire Competition Championship have come croppers over the professional laws, and will lose two points each, while Flunslet's case is just as bad in the Northern League and carries the same penalty. It will not take much more of this to cause open revolt against the working clause. Professionalism pure and simple seems to me to be coming along rapidly, and I am quite in accord with what Old Ebor says.

The well-known Yorkshire football scribe writes as following :—" There must come a time—and it is not far distant to my thinking—when clubs will put their heads together and say: This rule of No work no play' is beautiful in theory, most excellent in principle, but, inasmuch as you cannot make men sober by Act of Par- liament, neither can you make them work by football enactment. In other words, sooner or later, the Pro- fessional Sub-Committee, with its tons of waste paper usually called 4, permits " will be asked to cease its labours and give clubs and players a free hand in what they may do or may not do in the matter of employ. ment. I am not prepared to say that the moral effect of this will be for the better, although it certainly will make unnecessary the present system of organised de- ception and lying—for let it be plainly understood there is as much ingenuity shown now in defeating the professionalism -laws of the Northern Union as there I ever was in the days of veiled professionalism in the Rugby Union. What is really wanted is an elevation of the standard of club management. If our chief clubs were dominated by cool-headed men of the world as distinct from mere football enthusiasts, there would be no difficulty in controlling players and in club managers being freed from the charge of manufacturing loafers to play football. Club managers, by a judicious combination of firmness and moral suasion,can do what lam afraid the Professional Sub-Committee with its reams of permit papers will never accomplish. "

IShow of Chrysanthemums at Walton Lea. With his usual generosity Mr John Crosfleld h air again allowed the public to enter hie grounds se Walton Lea to view his collection of chrysan- themums. The grounds were open between the hours of two and five p.m. on Saturday, Sunday and Monday, and large numbers availed themselve- of the privilege, Thousands of visitors were pre sent on Sunday when there was a record attend- ance, such a large number never having been seen in the grounds on previous occasions. The attend- ance on Saturday and Monday was much smaller. Ine conduct of the visitors was admirable and Mr William Kipps, the head gardener, and his staff had no difficulty in maintaining order. The display of chrysanthemums eclipsed that of previous year in quantity, variety and excellence, and Mr Kipps is to be congratulated upon the success which has attended his cultiva- tion of the plants. The choicest b blooms were placed in the conservatory adjoining the house. The collection was remarkable tor the wealth of colour and the variety of blooms, especially in the Japanese varieties. Amongst the best blooms dis- played in this class may be mentioned the Florence Molyneux, an enormous white flower; the G C Schwabe, a carmine rose; the Graphic, a silvery rosy white; the Hairy Wonder, a bronze buff; the Joseph Chamberlain, a deep crimson; Lerd Lud- low, a golden amber with red lines on the margin of the florets; Lord Salisbury, a yellow suffused crimson; the Pride of Exmouth, white delicately shaded with pink; and the W R Church, a rosy crimson with bronze reverse. There wee some very pretty blooms in the incurved varieties notably the President Bevan, yellow, with rosy shadings, nne of the largest incurveds ever raised Mention must also be made of the smaller chrysan- themums known as pompoms,. ths Cedo white flower; the Elsie Walker, an orange brown, tipped yellow; the Rosinante, a blush rose; and the snowdrop, a pure white being the best. Not only were the visitors privileged to see such a choice collection of chrysanthemums, but they were also free to wander through the hot houses where orchids, begonias, primulas, ferns, grapes and pine- apples were to be seen growing.

Ile is progressing favourably.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
iA FATHER'S OFFENCE.-FAILING TO NOTIFY SCARLET FEVER. . _

Edward Kelly. 39. Lercester-street, was charged on a warrant at tde Warrington Police Court on Saturday with having failed to report to the Medical Officer of Health that his daughter was suffering from scarlet fever ; and also with having exposed the girl, to the danger of the public, whilst suffering from the disease.—The prisoner pleaded not guilty to both charges.—Mr Stanley Wilsoß (deputy town clerk) said that the school attendance officers were going their round and visited the house of the prisoner, who gave as an excuse for the child not attending school that she was suffer- ing from scarlet fever. The case was reported to the Medical Officer of Health, who visited the house and found the girl in the late or peeling stage of the fever. Prisoner said the child had been ill two months, and that the illness started with a red rash. He had sent her to school at various times,—That in his (31r Wilson's) opinion was the moat serious part of the case. She had made 80 attendances out of a possible 120 at the Sacred Heart Schools, Bank Quay. The magis- trates would see the danger of the child's having attended school, and at the present time there was in the Whitecross Ward an epidemic of fever, although they could not say that it was the result of the action of the defendant. The committee had con- sidered this case, and thought it should not be allowed to pass, but should be brought before the public to let them know what were their duties in such a matter. William Jones. school attendance officer, gave evidence corroborating Mr Wilson's statement. Miss Bonny, headmistress of the Sacred Heart Schools. Bank Quay, produced a return of the child's attendances at school.—Dr Gornall, Medical Officer of Health for the borough, said that from information he received be visited the house of prisoner on the 13th mat, He went in the morning but failed to gain admittance, although he was under the impression that there was some one in at the time. In the afternoon he went to the back of the house and met Prisoner just going in. He entered,and found the child suffering from scarlet fever as stated. It might have been ill for about six weeks, but prisoner's state- ment was to the effect that it had been suffering for two months. The attack had commenced with red rash. The father said he had taken the girl to the Infirmary, but as he had not a recommend he was refused treatment. He afterwards got a recommend, but had not used it. Witness took steps to have the child removed to the hospital, where it was at present. It was very Important that all cases should be got Into the hospital. Their failure to secure any considerable diwinution,—rhe Clerk : That has nothing to do with this case.—Mr Wilson : It is outside the case.—Dr Gornall : I was only going to point out the danger of these cases, that there are so many Cases we cannot account tor.—ame cramr- man said the Bench considered it a very serious case, as prisoner had not only endangered his own family but others. They had decided to fine him 20s including costs in each case, or in default 28 days' imprisonment.
SERIOUS CHARGE AT WARRINGTON.-ALLEGED FALSE PRETENCES.

At the Warrington Police Court on Saturday, before Messrs Hayward (in the chair) and R. T. Fairclough, Ralph Plant, jun., whose address was given as 15, Pitt-lane, Wool- &tauten. was charged with having on the 6th and 9th April, 1900, "with intent to defraud William Breward, unlawfully and knowingly by certain false pretences frandulently Induced him to accept certain valuable securities, to wit three bills of exchange, for the repayment of the respective sums of £24, £3O, and £3O 17s, contrary to the form of the statute in such case made and provided." Mr Browne appeared for Breward, and explained that his client was an earthenware dealer who carried on business in Buttermarket- street. and the defendant was formerly a member of the firm of Plant and Company. who carried on business as earthenware manufacturers in the Potteries. 61r Breward, on April 7th, received a wire from Plants to the effect that they had some good cheap lines to offer him if he was prepared to buy. He wired that he was prepared to buy if the price was low enough. Later on the same day Ralph Plant, jun . called upon him. He showed the invoices pro- duced, which were already made out, and related to nine crates of ware. He went through the invoices with hirn.and prisoner said the crates were at Longton station, and that he would allow complainant an extra 5 per cent, discount and take two bills for one and four months. Breward asked the prisoner why he was so anxious to sell, and he replied that they were paying out a partner, and had to find £350 by Saturday morn lug. The complainant agreed to purchase and prisoner drew the two bills of exchange which com- plainant endorsed. He afterwards saw his bankers, who advised him that he would not have to meet the bills if the goods were not delivered. The following Monday morning he received another wire from defendant stating that he had another lot better than the first, and asking complainant to meet him and his partner at Bank Quay station. He new became rather suspicious and again saw his bankers, who informed him that he would be all right If he purchased more crates provided he had an independent witness present. He and a friend went to the station and there met Mr ttalph Plant, jun., and another. Plant said he had some more stuff to off ar. and they then all went to complainant's house, where the two invoices were produced. After reading them he told the prisoner he did not want No. 18 crate, as he had plenty of the ware it contained. He said the whole of the crates were lying at Longt on Station. and it was solely upon that statement Complainant agreed to take the lot at a discount ot 5 per cent extra, and the defendant drew two bills, one for £3O in four months, and the other for £3O 17s at five months. Complainant subsequently received from the Railway Com- pany three crates. The first was right to invoice, the second differed in contents, but contained about right value, and the third was considerably below value. He wrote Plants about the third crate and received no reply. He went to the Potteries and saw Ralph Plant jun. who said that some of the crates had got a bit mixed, but that their packer had been to the station and had put them right, and that the balance of the crates were at the station waiting complain- ant's instructions. He would put in another crate for the one below value. Complainant went to the station and found there were no crates, and a week after the prisoner filed his petition, with the result that the complainant had lost the whole of £9O which had almost been his ruin.— Prisoner went away to America, but recently returned and surrendered himself to the police.—The prisoner was remanded until to-day (Saturday) when he will be legally represented.

Mos/DAL—Before Mr F Monks (in the chair), Alderman Sutton, Councillor Smethurst and Messrs Birchall, Hay- ward. Thornton and Wright. WAS IT CIIRONIC LAMENESS ?—CONFLICT OF EvIDENCE IN AN R.S.P.C.A. CAsk.—Michael Hessen, carter, was summoned for cruelty to a horse on the 16th inst by work- ing it when it was in an unfit condition, and Thomas Lowe. Sankey Hall farm was summoned for allowing the horse to be worked —Mr Browne appeared for the defendants and pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Corbett said he saw the defendant Hessen driving a horse attached to a lorry containing 28 bags of oats in Arpley-road: He noticed that the animal was lame and sweating. He asked Hessen who had author- ised him to yoke the horse to the lurry, and he said his master, Mr Lowe, had 'lent him out with the horse. He added that he was going to Garton's Seed Warehouse Witness watched him go into the yard, and afterwards brought Inspectors Print and Robinson to the plane. The horse was then taken out of the lorry, and with great diffi- culty taken to the Seven Stars yard. The animal was very lame.—Cross-examined : Hessen did not tell him that the horse had slipped coming down the Central Station-hill. He heard that subseduenzly the horse was shot.—lnspector Print RSPC A, said the horse was lame on both hind legs front spavin. It was exceedingly lame on the off hind limb and was suffering intense pain. The ihock was very hot and inflamed and very tender to the touch. Mr Lowe admitted to him that he knew the animal was suffering from a Chronic disease and could not be cured. The animal Was destroyed.— Mr Browne said that Mr Lowe had had this horse for two years and prior to this it had never had a particle of lameness. On the morning mentioned he saw it go out. It was not lame then. It was drawing a load of oats from the Central Station to Messrs Garton's, and going down the gradiant from the station slipped and hurt itself. Reason had great difficulty in getting the horse to Friar's-green. Mr Lowe was informed and upon the advice of his veterinary surgeon, Mr Hewitt, he had the animal destroyed. The magistrates mr:st find That there was intentional cruelty or such want of ordinary

oversight as would have prevented the cruelty.—Mr Lowe gave evidence in support. Questioned by Inspector Print as to whether he did not say tte should plead guilty and send a cheque for the fine, he replied that he said he might do:— Hessen said he told the police officer that the horse had slipped.—Thomas Brown, horsekeeper and yard foreman,Baid he had driven the horse for eighteen months and it had not been lame during that time. His master did not permit him to let horses out that were lame and held him re3pon- sible for any disobedience.—The magistrates recalled P.C. Corbett and ascertained from him that he had seen the horse slightly lame a fortnight before he stopped it.—Mr Browne said it was absolutely illegal to recall the constable and to ask these questions.—Mr Monks said they had a per- fect right to recall him —Mr Browne : Your Clerk will advise you have not.—Mr Lowe was fined Ss and costs and the case against Hessen was dismissed. MECEITTNG MILITARY BOOTS.—Rdward Reardon, Black- hurst-street.was charged with receiving two pairs of military boots from Henry Reardon. a private in the Ist Battalion of the Royal Lancashire Fusiliers. on November 16 He pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable said that the prisoner was charged under the Army Act, of 1881, which prohibited any man from receiving any of the equipment of a soldier. About half-past ten o'clock on Tuesday morning Superintendent Monaghan and Detective Barlow were on duty in Mersey-street, and saw the prisoner coming along with aoreething bulky under his coat. When asked what it was, he said he had a pair of boots, which were his, and added, 'Do you think I have stolen them ? " He did not satisfy the officers, however, and was brought to the police station. It was then discovered he had two pairs of boots which belonged to his brother, who had given them to him to pledge. There was no excuse of ignorance of the law for the prisoner, i for not only was his brother a soldier, but he also had been a soldier.— Sergeant Atherton from the barrack said that one of the first things told a soldier when he enlisted was that he was not to part with his equipment. - A fine of 40s, including costs, or one month in default, was Imposed.

div.head: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A HAYDOCK MAN. Alleged Unlawful Wounding.
div.p: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A HAYDOCK MAN. Alleged Unlawful Wounding.

At the Warrington Occasional Court on Monday, before Mr. John White, Peter Casey, 362, Millfield-road, Haydock, was charged with unlawfully wounding his wife Elizabeth on the 9.-h inst., by striking her on the bead with a basin.

_ Eiizabeth Casey, wife of the prisoner, stated that on the date in question her husband came home under the influence of drink. They began to quarrel, and prisoner called her foul names. She then hit him on the head with a tin can, After she had &Are so prisoner pieked up a basin or pot and threw it at her, and it struck her on the head. Prisoner then knocked her down. She got up and ran out of the house. Prisoner followed her and knocked her down in the road. She did not remember anything until she found herself in a neigh- bour's house. She was bleeding from a wound on the back of the head. Dr B G Henderson said he saw Mrs Casey in the afternoon and she was suffering from a wound on the back of the head, three quarters of an inch long. Toe wound was bleeding very freely and the woman was in a very feeble condition through loss of blood. An artery had been severed. Mrs Casey was also bruised about the shmlder and left arm, and this might have been caused by the chsgs produced. She had been under his care ever since and had been confined to her bed until last Friday. Walter Topping, blacksmith, 14, Peel-road, Haydock, said that shortly after dinner time he was in Millfield- lane and saw Mrs Casey come out of the house bleeding from a wound on the head. Prisoner, who appeared to have had a good deal of drink, followed her. He had a jug in his hand and threw it at her, but it did not strike her. Mrs Casey fell and prisoner came up and "gave her a knock or two" with his hand. Witness did not see him kick her,and he did not notice whether prisoner was wearing clogs or boots. Other evidence was called,the witnesses including P C Johnson, who apprehended the prisoner. When appre- hended he was wearing the clogs produced and was under the influence of drink. Oa being charged prisoner said" That statement is wrong. Did you see me hit her with a basin?
Prisoner said he was drunk and was sorry for what bad occurred. He denied that lie was wearing the clogs. He was committed to the Liverpool AsEizes for trial.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
THE NORTHERN LEAGUE.
WARRINGTON'S HARD LUCK AT HALIFAX.

Warrington made another journey into Yorkshire Oa Saturday when they played Halifax at Hanson-lane before 5,000 people. The weather was the best possible for football. and the ground also being in order a fast game was witnessed Both teams turned out as advertised though Fish was still absent from the Warrington ranks. Mr J H Smith should have refereed, but he did not turn up and Mr Renton of Hunsiet officiated. The te ims were as follows : Halifax.—Little, back ; Nicholl, Rigg. Lewis., and Arnold, three-quarter backs ; Morley and Joe Riley. half backs ; Bartle, Jack Riley, Kitson, Heap, Morton, Langloorn,

Hammond and Swinbank, forwards Warrington.—Hallam, back; Hockenball, Isherwood. Dickenson, and Harris, three-quarter backs ; Allen and Burgess half-backs ; Morrison, Boardman, Fell, Edmond- son, F Swift, Jolley, Eden, and W Swift, forwards. Kitson started the game for Halifax and after exchanges. Little took a penalty kick from near midfied, but failed at goal. Isherwood responded with a good run and punted across to Harris, who failed to gather the ball. Burgess got away and a passing run by Dickenson and Harris took play well into the home quarter, where the wing man was brought down by Arnold. A mull by Lewis nearly let War- rington in, keen play taking place in front of the Halifax goal. The Warrington backs passed across smartly. theism- ' son losing the ball which was taken over by Harris, but a scrimmage was ordered. Riley relieved the pressure with a punt to centre. Warrington were soon on the attack again, the forwards following Dickenson's kick up so well as to prevent another return. Another passing bout was initiated but the final transfer to Harris went wrong, a good chance being missed. Give and take movements followed, Hallam being cheered for fine defensive play. A penalty kick against ',Warrington was the means of Halifax attacking. Little dropping at goal and missing the mark by inches only. Warrington soon cleared their line, Rigg being grassed at centre by Eden. Dickenson and Harris again got away finely, the wing man clearing all but Little,who tackled StrOr gly. Arnold retaliated with a fast sprint into the War- ringtoa half, finally kicking across the goal mouth, where Jack Riley missed an easy try, Hockenhall making the ball dead. Even plry followed, and just before the interval Burgess was off owing to injuries, but resumed. At half- time there was no score. J Swift resumed and Halifax assumed the aggressive. Bad fielding by Isher wood gave them a footing in the War- rington half and by easy stages they worked the ball to the line. Here aiscrimmage was fought out and Joe Riley dodged over with an easy try five minutes from the restart. Little improved with a good goal-kick. Warrington rallied finely and immediately rushed to the other end, where Allen go hold and passed to Isherwood who romped past Nicholl and scored. Hallam equalised with a fine oblique shot. Pia y was now fast and furious, Halifax having rather the best of matters owing to the clever way in which the forwards wheeled the scrummages. Arnold and Little both dropped sr, goal but failed. tbe full back's attempt being a very rine one from toucri. Warrington derenned west. out Joe was only just kept out by Morrison on one occasion. Ha._ had a penalty shot at goal and failed by only a little, while in the course of a sharp attack Harris kicked across, the home custodian only just saving. Powerful punting by Little drove Warrington back, Dickenson making a strong run to centre. Halifax were soon back again, Rigg being brought down on the line after a smart piece of combination. A free kick temporarily gave relief to WarringtOn, but the Halifax forwards carried play to the line again. There was a general melee and Morley was awarded a very doubtful try five minutes from time. Little failed at goal. Warrington made great efforts to get on even terms agaln,but the defence prevailed and the whistle sounded with Halifax victors by one goal two tries (eight points) to Warrington one goal one try (five points).

div.head: SWINTON JUST BELT RUNCORN.
div.p: SWINTON JUST BELT RUNCORN.

There wee only a moderate attendance of spectators at Swin:on to witness the match between these clubs. Run- corn played as selected, but on t he Swinton side Cooper appeared in place of Lewis who had not recovered from the Injury he received in the Hunslet match. From start to finish the game was stubbornly contested, and it was only towards the close that Swinton managed to turn an ap- parent defeat into a win by three points. Runcorn began to ' attack strongly from the kick-off, and the game had only been in progress a short time when Jolley got the ball from a scrummage and dropped a goal, Runcorn continued to hove the beet of matters, mainly through their forwards opening out and preventing the Swinton combination from getting to work. and although Chorley drove them back time after time,Swlnton were unable to score before the interval. Hods were changed with Runcorn leading by two points. In the second hell the game underwent a complete change, Swinton commenced to attack vigorously, and a fine passing Movement between their three-quarters should have resulted In a try, but unfortunately Cooper placed his foot in touch at the Runcorn line. Houghton played a capital game, and although he was several times tackled by Messer before he could get rid of the ball, it was mainly through his strong defence that Swinton were kept so long from scoring. It was towards the finish when a combined movement of the Swinton backs ended In Cooper getting- possession, and he kicked the ball over Houghton's head and then placed his men on side. Rvans nipped it up and scored a try, which Messer improved, and the game ended :—Swinton, one goal and one try (five points) ; Runcorn, one goal (two.points).

div.head: BROUGIZTON RANGERS' FIRST REPEAT.
div.p: BROUGIZTON RANGERS' FIRST REPEAT.

The Rangers journeyed to Hunslet to play the return match with that club, and for the first time this season they suffered defeat. In the first match at Broughton, Hunslet showed such indifferent form and were BO easily beaten that the result of the return match was looked upon as a fore- gone conclusion. The defeat therefore came as a great sur- prise. A Goldthorpe kicked off for Hunslet and early on the Rangers were penalised twice, but A Goldthorpe failed to take advantage of the place kicks. Then the Rangers got going and Wilson kicked the ball to Walker, who. on being tackled, lost possession and Reynolds scored a try for the Rangers, which W James improved. After this reverse Hunslet attacked strongly and Whiteley and Smith scored tries both of which A Goldthorpe improved. The Rangers. also scored again and at the interval the score was ten points each. On resuming Hunslet at once began to attack, and but for the strong defensive play of Fielding and Hogg would have scored in the first few minutes. They, however, con- tinue I for a time to hold the upper hand of the Rangers,and, from a pass by A Goldthorpe, Robinson dropped a goal. Several times the Rangers carried play close to the home line and their backs made many passing movements, but these were never allowed to take effect, owing to the strong defensive play of the II unslet backs, and only minor points resulted. Robinson scored another try for Hunslet,which A Goldthorpe improved, and when "no side was called, the Rangers had suffered their first defeat. Score : Hunslet, four goals and three tries (17 points) ; Broughton Rangers, two goals and two tries (ten points).

Salford then took up the attack, and from a scrummage inside the Leigh quarter, Lomas got away and passed the ball to Varty, who scored an unimproved try, The game had ecatcely started again when Slolyneux threw the ball well out to Johnson. who scored an unimproved try G tricaked pass from riffiths the ball over his tfoorvvLielilgiahm. s.Drua nu btaav Si am ith. next ainndtetrhceenp head, but in the race for possession Smith beat Dunbavin and thus saved a'certain try to Salford.!At half-time the score was three points each. In the second half, Lomas opened the scoring with a fine try, and the same player, a few minutes later, made a capital opening for Griffiths to score, and LOMA& kicked a goal. With a lead of eight points Sal- ford eased a little. but Leigh failed to take advantage of many good openings, chiefly through poor combination, and the game ended :—Salford, one goal and three tries (eleven points) ; Leigh one try (three points).
HUDDERSFIELD V. OLDHAM.

Vrater started this match at Hudderfield. Dewhurst returning. Kitchen took the play to the Oldham quarter, but their backs relieved by passing. Larard and Kitchen by fine play brought the ball back, but Lees relieved with a penalty. Play now degenerated into the kick-and-mark order, until Lhrard made a fine burst, which Deere spoiled by failing to take his pass Oldham returned and Vowles scored, Lees converting. Half-time :—Oldham. 13 points ; Huddersfield, nil. After the interval Driver re- started,and Deere made a fine effort, but was held ; Dewhurst next dribbled to the line, but Thomas kicked dead. Huddersfield returned to the attack. and Deere scored. Oldham then rushed down and Brady scored, Huzzey failing. The Huddersfield forwards next went over in a body, a minor resulting. Kitchen, kicked a goal from a penalty, and De.re also scored, the result being :—Oldham, two goals and five tries (19 points) : Huddersfield, one goal and two tries (eight points.)

BATLEY V. BRA DFORD. At Batley. Soon after Spurr hal kieked off for Batley smart passing by the Bradford three-quarters enabled Pollard to cross his opponents' line, but Cooper made a poor attempt at goal. The Batley forwards rushed the ball half the length of the field, but Wilford failed at goal. Frona a penalty kick Batley continued to press, but Cooper at length brought relief. Garner was next conspicuous by a good run, and while Ward was tackling him Goodall got posses- sion, and without any opposition put the ball behind the posts. Fitzgerald failed at goal. The game became fast and exciting, and Oakland scored a try for Batley, Judge scoring a goal. Half time i—Satley, one goal an Lwo tries ; Brad- ford, one try. This engagement was decided on the ground a the former team. Richardson was very prominent for the visitors, and crossed the line after smart paseing, but the point was dis- allowed. Then Smith scored, no goal resulting. Half-time : Rochdale, three points; Fletcher Russells, nil. Result : Rochdale Hornets, eleven points ; Fletcher Russells, nil.
WARRINGToN " A " v. BIRKENHEAD WANDERERS "-4112.

This match was played on the Wilderspool enclosure. During the first part of the game Birkenhead pressed and after a splendid round of passing among the three quarters the visitors registered their first try. No goal resulted Even play followed, and Warrington by good forward work got near the line. Townson got possession and forcing his way through his opponents put the ball behind the posts Ratcliffe failed at goal. Birkenhead again became aggressive and scored. Ralf time, Birkenhead 6 points Warrington 3. On resuming scrambling play ensued and the game was very uninteresting for some time. At length Ratcliffe taking a pass from Duckworth ssored after a good run, and also kicked a goal. Birkenhead were now hard pressed and Knight scored for Warrington from a forward rush, Ratcliffe converting. Smart passing resulted in Birken- head scoring, Near the close passing among the backs ended in Taylor scoring for Warrington' Final, Warrington 2 goals 4 tries (16 points), Birkenhead 1 goal, 3 tries (11 points.)
RUNCORN A_ v. SWINTON A.

These teams met on the Runcorn ground on Saturday afternoon before a fair attendance of spectators. At the out- set Runcorn pressed. and Faulkner would have scored but for bad passing. Swinton then visited the Runcorn quarters and Wallwork scored, J Valentine kicking a goal. A mull by White resulted in Wallwork again scoring. The game continued to be of a ding-dong character, and after some hot work in the visitors' quarter, Williams placed a goal for Runcorn from a penalty.—Runcorn played much better from this point, and the visitors had all their work out out in pre- venting them from adding to their score. Half-time : Swinton, eight points; Runcorn, two. On the change of ends the game was warmly c natested. The visitors scored two more tries and at length ran out winners by 14 points to two.

div.head: LANCASHIRE LEAGUE.
div.p: LANCASHIRE LEAGUE.

EARLESTOWS V. PREscoT. At Prescot, in pleasant weather. The home team were responsible for the opening rnovemeats, but Clarke and Henry did not make Very much impression on Earlestown's defence. The visitors then became extremely aggressive. and their left wings.. Leach and Settle, severally tested Prescot's defence, which proved shaky. Soon afterwards the visitors left again obtained possession. Settle passing to Leach, and beating Leather squarely. Green dashed up to the rescue, but made a very poor show, and Leach, passing him easily, let drive at Johnson, who also failed to respond, and the leather found the corner of the net. Resuming, the visitors still had the best of matters until Thompson and Morgan made tracks for Chew. and Morgan's final kick sent the leather a yard wide of the enemy's post. Barlestown again Invaded Prescot 's territory, but found Green and Woodward ready. The remaining Rarlestown forwards joined in the fray, which was very adjacent to Johnson, and matters looked ominous till Leather chipped in and relieved. Present then went away smartly on the left, and some excellent passing was exhibited be• tween Thompson, Henry, and Horgan, so that Rarlestown suffered severe Pressure, and ultimately Chew fisted out a roaster from Henry. Both sets of forwards now put in speedy work, and both ends were visited rapidly in turn. Bradley took the ball well nigh to the corner flag, and shot across to Settle on the other wing, but Green anticipated the pass smartly, and a smart kick put his men in posses- sion. Henry was soon robbed by Whitehouse. who gave to Dawson. He, with Settle, made a 'stubborn effort to break through, but failed to pass Woodward, and the pressure was relieved. Half time : Earlestown one goal ; Preston. nil. Leach scored the second goal for Harlestown. but Prescot had hard lines in not scoring. Final : Barlestewn, two goals ; Prescot, nil.

NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS V. BLNGOR.

At Newton on Saturday. Both teams were wall repre- sented. Newton won the toss, and Jones kicked off down the field for Bangor. Mar was very evenly contested by both teams, who pressed in turn. Bangor eventually came down with a rush, and an exciting few minutes was seen in the home goal. The home left wing broke away, and play was contested in the visitors' half. Bangor again ran down, and after grand Passing, R Owen Score the opposing custodian not having the slightest chance to save. Immedi- atels afterwards Bangor ran down, add for a short time play WAS contested in the Newton half' The bomesters brake away at length, and after neat passing, Ellison equalised the scores with a fine shot. A misunderstanding ion the part of the Newton backs proved fatal, as Ba.Jgor scored their second goal. The ground was very hard and slippery in emsequenco of the recent rain and frost. Lewis scored a third point for Bangor, who dis- played better finish to their play than the homesters Newton tried hard to increase their score, but Bangor offered a stubborn resistance. Notwithstanding this Butler found an opening, and netted the ball In grand style. Half- time :—Bangor, three goals ; Newton-le-Willows, two. In the second half, Newton had much the better of the game, and added two goals to their opponents one, the match thus terminating in a draw.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Methodist Free. Churche Buckley-
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Methodist Free. Churche Buckley-
street.

On Sunday afternoon a musical service was given in the Methodist Free Church, Buckley-street, by the Legh- street Primitive Methodist choir. Mr a Taylor presided. An excellent programme was submitted by the choir, who,under the able leadership of Mr A Spruce,acquitted themselves with great credit. Their singing was excel- lent and was much enjoyed by a large congregation. The anthems sung were " Lead, kindly Light " and "Teach me, 0 Lord," and the choruses "And the Glory" and the" Gloria." I quartette was contributed by the Misses Bridge and Woodland and Messrs Corrin and Spruce, a duet by the Misses Hewitt and Spruce. and solos by Miss A Bridge and Messrs J Corrin and A Spruce. Mr F Podmore presided at tie organ.
Temperance Sunday at the Free Churches in Warrington.

At most of the Free Churches and Sunday schools on Sunday reference was made to the subject of Temper- ance, it being Temperance Sunday. At Wycliffe Con- gregational Church, on Sunday evening, the pastor, Rev. John Yonge, preached a special sermon on the subject "Abstinence from intoxicating beverages—a necessity for many, a harm to nobody, a duty for all." He based his remarks on the text contained in Roman s , 14 c, 19 v. He wished to urge upon everyone, he said, the personal duty of abstaining from the use of bever- ages which intoxicate. He was not going to say that alcohol could never be useful and therefore never per. missible. There had been and there still was consider- able medical and scientific dispute upon that point. He was not going to discuss it. It was absolutely cer- tain that the medical profession to-day did not prescribe the use of alcohol co anything like the extent that was formerly the case. It was not the medicinal use of alcohol that caused so much drunken- ness, but the use of intoxicating drinks as beverages. There were many Christian people,who by the continual use of these dangerous beverages and who never got over the line themselves, encouraged the use to those whom such beverages brought danger, than disaster, death and damnation. That was the darkest shame of all. In referring to the first part of his subject that total abstinence from intoxicating beverages was for many a positive necessity, the preacher cited instances showing how many who were what were called "moder- ate drinkers " ultimately became habitual drunkards owing to the power which drink exercised over them. There was no safety in any other course than that of total abstinence. In dealing with the second point, Mr Yonge contended that the giving up of a beverage was not much after all. Hs pointed out that total abstainers were never afflicted with thirst whilst on the ether hand an intoxicating beverage created thirst. To ask a man to give up drinking beer was not to ask him to do anything that would imperil his strength. it had been proved beyond all doubt that total abstainers lived longer than those who took intoxicating drink.lt would do parents no harm to give up the use of intoxicating beverages and on the other hand by their example they might save their children from becoming drunkards. In conclusion the preacher urged that it was a duty for all as patriots hiving the welfare of the country at 'heart. At Bold-street Wesleyan Church there vete large congregations. The preacher in the morning was the Rev W C J Neville.who was listened to with marked attention. In the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev T Bishop who spoke on "The sting in the wine cup." He gave some interesting particulars, with re- gard to drink and its effects. At the usual gathering of men and women of the Byrom-hall P.S.A. Society,Liver- pool, the Rev F G West occupied the chair. The Rev J Fi Matthews (Latchford) gave a stirring temperance address, it being Temperance Sunday.

div.head: AN EXPENSIVE WORD.
div.p: AN EXPENSIVE WORD.

It has cost Great Britain a hundred millions sterling (£100,000,000) to write that two-lettered word ex which now stands in front of President Kruger's name: and she is now spending a few pounds more, tinkering at the hyphen which connects it with the word President. This is the most expensive writing the world has ever seen—fifty millions sterling per letter ! But this is a strange way of stating a fact. There is nothing remarkable in a man signing his name ; but when it is done by Mr Pierpoint Morgan to a cheque in payment for a mercantile fleet,or by a judge on a death warrant, there is much significance in it. To be out of health is a serionS misfortune to any man or woman, even when they can afford every comfort. To those whose daily lot it is to toil, sickness is a calamity ; it is as full of meaning to them as that little word ex is to Oam Paul, which it has cost John Bull so much to tack on to hi a name.

Mrs Annie Goudie is a widow, and lives with her son at 29, Newhall-street, Bridgeton, Glasgow, and works in a weaving mill near her home. " Between five and six years ago," said Mrs ;Goudie on the 7th September, 1901, " I tell into a bad state of health. I had never been a great eater,but now my appetite almost left me,and the little I ate,occasioned me great pain. The chief trouble seemed to be in my chest and stomach but I frequently suffered great pain between the shoulders. My nerves became badly affected, aad I felt weak and generally unfit. A doct3r whom I saw gave me some temporary relief, but I was soon as bad again as ever. While in this wretched state, I had the good fortune to meet with a little book.and by reading it I was induced to buy a bottle of S3igel's Syrup. This medicine afforded me almost instant relief, and by persevering with it I very soon became well. Now and then I still have slight attacks of my malady, but Seigel's Syrup never fails to set me right again." Su3h is the testimony of a perfectly reliable honest woman who has expressed her gratitude for the benefit she has derived from Seigel's Syrup, and given per- misoion for her experience of its efficacy to be published.

Whatever the rights and wrongs of the long: drawn- out South African conflict, and whatever the complica- tions of the political world in the near future, it is highly improbaVe Paul Kruger will ever be able to expunge the ex which John Bull has prefixed to his former style and dignity. But health is better than power—indeed it is the greatest sf powers, for without it all else counts for nothing. In our Carnegie Competition we have awarded One Guinea to the following :—J 13 Newton, 22, Armley Lodge-road, Armley.Leeds ; William R Jones, Cwmrrfel, Nr Llangadock. Carmarthenshire ; John Blyth, c/o J L Gammie, 41, Duff-street, Macduff, N.B. ; Mrs Sarah Whit, West Ead, Steeple Claydon, Winslow ;E M Hardwick, Nether Silton, Northallerton. Further awards will be announced in the newspapers from week to week.

THE CYCLE nuns is LIVERPOOL.—In Liverpool cycle trade circles, a change has taken place within the last few weeks, the most important being the establish- ment of a local depot by Messrs Humber, Limited. The firm had taken a spacious and handsome shop in Bold- street (the Holborn Viaduct of Liverpool), and a well- known and experienced local cycle trader has been ap- pointed manager of the new depot. The shop taken by Messrs Humber is one of the largest and handsomest cycle establishments in the North. It was for many years occupied by the well-known Liverpool agents, Messrs Slade and Co., and on Mr Slade, sen., retiring from business, it was taken over by the John Griffiths Cycle Corporation, and later on by the Cycle and Motor Co. Mr R Maclennan, the gentleman whom Messrs Humber have appointed their Liverpool manager,served I his apprenticeship to Mr Slade, and many of the earlier years of his life were spent in the shop of which he has now been given the management. Mr Maclennan is one of the oldest and most experienced cycle traders in Liverpool. He is a prominent member of the local tralers' association, aud very popular with his brother traders. He is thoroughly au fait with Humber cycles, having been interested in the sale of them for many years, latterly in his capacity as manager of the Bold- street shop of Messrs HitchingS,Limited, whose agencies included the Humber.
ROBBERIES AT WARRINGTON.
Three Public houses; a House and a Shop Entered.

A series of impudect robberies was perpetrated at Warrington on Sunday and Monday evenings. Three public houses and a dwelling house were entered on Sunday evening and valuables were stolen. and the following night a shop was visited in like manner. The matter is in the hands of the poliee but, up to the present, the depredator or depredators have not been discovered.

The first public house to receive a visit seems to have been the Barley Mow Inn, in the Market-place, of which Mr James Gleava is the landlord, The thief had entered the back-yard some time after half-past five,and found a ladder convenient for his purpose. This he placed against a small window at the rear of the pre- mises, and thus secured an entrance, and got into the bedroom of Miss Hill, the barmaid, from which was ' stolen a purse, a sovereign, and a gold ring. The robbery was discovered about seven o'clock, but no [trace could be found of the thief.

At a quarter to eight it was discovered that the Mid- land Hotel, Horsemarket-street, bad been entered, and that the thief or thieves had made a substantial "haul." The robbery took place some time after six o'clock. when the articles ' were seen safe in the bedroom. The articles stolen consisted of a lady's gold hunter watch with engraved case, and with a black enamelled flower at the back ; a lady's long gold small link chain with an American 20 dollar piece attached ; a gentleman's fetter link gold albert ; a square gold locket with compass set,with diamonds,containing photographs of Mr and Mrs Wake- field, and with name and age inscribed on the back; the total value of which is estimated at £5O. Another robbery was perpetrated at the "Gross Keys" Hotel, Butterrnarket-street. It appears that the thief climbed over the adjoining school wall, and suc- ceeded in gaining admission to the front bedroom by means of the lavatory window. A small light was burn- ing in the room at tile time, but this the thief turned full on, presumably to assist him in his search for valuables, A drawer, which had been previously locked, was force open, from which was taken £2 ss. in silver, also a pair of valuable gold earrings belonging to Mrs Anderton. The theft appears to have been com- mitted about seven o'clock, and a few -ninutes later, Mr. Anderton, the proprietor, came from below and proceeded upstairs in order to get his coat. He found the drawer forced open, and it EC.111113 that the thief being disturbed, took refuge in the lavatory. Mr. Anderton thinking a member of the family was present went downstairs and acquainted his wife with the state of affairs. This gave the thief his opportunity and he then made good his escape. The same evening the house of Mr. Cosgrove, Marsh House-lane, was entered and a purse containing 37s and several other articles were stolen.
On Mouday evening the premises occupied by Mr. J. Grooms, practical watchmaker and jeweller, 4, Church- street, were broken into, and £5 in money and two watches stolen.

Is the latest example of the benefits of cc-operation. Like the " North Mail" in the north-east, and the " Midland Express" in the midlands, it will be run in co-operation with the London "Express." This means that, both at home and abroad, it will have facilities for obtaining news which cannot possibly exist in the case of a lecal paper standing alone.

NORTH EXPRESS. The first column of the NORTH EXPRESS will consist of a bright, snappy summary of the world's news under the heading " To-day's Story." This will enable the reader to gather briefly the whole contents of the paper in a couple of minutes. The NORTH EXPRESS will also obtain the special contributions written for the London " Ex- press" by the famous authors and experts who are continually contributing to its columns. Among them in the past have been Rudyard Kipling, Marie Corelli, Rider Haggard, Lord Charles Beresford, Lady Warwick, and a host of others almost equally renowned. The future will see writers of similar eminence represented in the NORTH EXPRESS. READ ON

div.head: NORTH EXPRESS.
div.p: THE NORTH EXPRESS.

has at great expense been connected with London by private wires. Every night these wires will carry to the NORTH EXPRESS the special news which bas been obtained for it and for the London "Express," by their own correspondents all over the world. So the NORTH EXPRESS will be in the position of having its own special representative everywhere, and will thus obtain an unrivalled ser- vice of news,
READ ON
READ ON

div.head: NORTH EXPRESS.
div.p: THE NORTH EXPRESS.

Talking about this latest development of journalistic enterprise the " Caxton Magazine" said the other day : " Where the country or localised edition of the London paper scores is in the fact that it is able to give its readers the benefit of a special news service, which in the nature of things must be infinitely superior to the best which can be afforded by its local rivals, at a cost to itself of practic- ally nothing at all. The news is cabled from all over the world to the London paper, and is then sent on to the country office. Thus the cost of it, and the heavy charges of transmission from abroad, have only to be borne once. What this means may be best appreciated when we say tbat many a cable addressed during this war to the offices of London newspapers has cost two or three hundred pounds for transmission. The advantage, then, in this respect is obvious and immense. Again, these country editions are being run on the smartest London lines, Some people say that this kind of journalism, as a substitute for the good, old-fashioned, solid sort of thing to which we have been accustomed, is to he deplored. Whether that is so or not, it is certain that the general public likes the new style, and is prepared to pay for it in preference to any other. It realises that it consists of brains and ideas."
