Wycliffe not only denied the eternal validity of Papal supremacy ; not only declared the Pope fallible ; not only declared the civil power justified in touching church revenues ; but he asserted that priests had no power, of themselves, to do either good or harm. "No man in reality is at all the better for the priest's bene- diction, nor the worse for his anathema.' Wycliffe re- jected:the"claim which",saidihe,"makes men into gods;" and he proclaimed it false, urging men to study the scripture and learn the truth for themselves. Would the Rector of Warrington do that ? If so why did he not belong to the British and Foreign Bible Society ?
AE DOCTRINE OF THE REAL PRESENCE..

- - Wycliffe testified against Papal powerlin its temporal phase. He bore witness against the unscriptural pre- tensions of the priesthood, who claimed to forgive sins by their own act and to consign to perdition in the same way. He gave to his countrymen the Bible. They could not therefore be surprised that he should at length fall foul of the question of - the Eucharist and the Papal doctrine of transubstautiatioa. Wycliffe admitted that the words of consecration did confer a peculiar, even mysterious dignity upon the bread and wine. But without any ambiguity, he laid down that those ele- ments were not to be considered " as Christ or any part of Him " but only "an effectual sign of Him." The Rector said that if there was anybody who loved to believe in the Real Presence alter and owing to consecration it was Wycliff s. Was what was supposed by High Anglicans to be the Real Presence only a sign ? If the Lord was really present in the sacramental bread .and wine after the words of consecration then surely those elements were infinitely more than signs. But Wycliffe said they were •• effec- tual signs" and nothing more. Then Wycliffe did not love to believe in the Real Presence after and owing to consecration. With all respect and esteem for the Rector, he was bound by Wycliffe's own words and not by the Rector's assertions of Wycliffe's views. Having dealt with Wycliffe's further career, the lecturer said they Would feel that although he was not a Congrega- tionalist nor a Nonconformist his views of religious freedom, of the place of Scripture in relation to faith, and his opposition to sacerdotal claims and pretentioas, placed him very manifestly on the ground which they (Congregationalists and Nonconformists) occupied tc- day. He ventured also to think that if John Wycliffe could himself re-appear his surprise, of which the Rector spoke last week, would be pleasurable to him rather than the reverse. He fancied his more real surprise I would be chat the Rector should put in a claim to him in the way he did. The whole of Wycliffe's conspicuous , contentions were identical with their's (Congregational- ists). They Were not nearly so identical with the Rector's.
" CHURCH " INSTEAD Or " CHAPEL."

• I believe, continued the lecturer, John Wycliffe snuld feel no difficulty in occupying the pulpit in Wycliffe Church. I believe also he would not object to our calling the building a" church "instead of a" chapel." With all respect for the Rector of Warrington I claim that we have as much right to call our place of worship a" church" as he has to call St Elphin's a "church," and we may even think be rather takes something of a liberty when he so pointedly refuses to speak of our sanctuary by the title which we prefer. What does it matter even if Dissenters of 50 years ago did notlase the word "church" to denote their buildings for worship ? These are days of progress and advance- ments. We do not call all things to-day by just the same names we did in days gone by. Dissenters of the early days used to build their places of worship in out of the way places because no others were obtainable. They built them in a very severe plainness of style that came partly by lack of means, perhaps somewhat of lack of taste, possibly also of a somewhat narrow and puritanical idea of what is seemly in worship and per- haps even from a deficiency of desirable self-assertive- ness. But we build in the front to-day. And we are willing and able to erect comely structures, worthy to take their Places beside churches like St Paul's or even St Elphin's. Moreover, we know that the word "church " as applied to a building for religious wor- ship simply means " the Lard's." It is derived from the Greek word " Kuriakc "—i.e., " the Lard's." It means that the building is for the honour and glory of God in His worship by His people. Also we know that the word " chapel," to which the Rector would seem to wish to reduce us, is originally " a place for a hat." It is said that the Kings of France, in war, carried Si Martin's bat into the field w'aich was kept in a tent as a precious relic, whence the place took the name " Capella," a little hat,and the priest who had the custody of the ten was called " capellanus," now "chaplain." This being the deriva- tion of the name chapnl, we do not quite see to its special aptitude to denote a place ot worship, even though many hats of many fashions are put there: aWn d e think the word "church " is better for the purpose than " chapel " it is shorter than meeting-house it is certainly more seemly than " conventicle." Hence we shall csrtainly adhere to it. The Rector, however, falls into a very easy confusion of ideas in his remarks on this point. He glides away from the name " church as applied to the religious community, and says that it never until recently has been so used. I beg to differ from him. Congregationalists and Baptists at any rate, have always spoken of their fellowships as
THE FATAL;TY TO A DEAF MUTE

1 " churches," and in doing so they follow strictly upon, Apostolic precedent. The assemblies of disciples always bore that name and in its primary and early Christian use, as meaning the assembly of disciples. Congrega- tionalists and B iptists, am o in fact the only true High Churchmen.- They believe the fellow- ship of believers, which is the Church, to be the supreme authority in matters pertaining to the Kingdom of God. The Church is self-governing, electing its own members and officers and ministers and managing its own saairs. It is a misuse of language for Anglicans to call themselves High Churchmen. With them the fellowship of believers is not recognized in any capacity of authority. They are High Saoramentarians, High Sacerdotalists, but they are not High Churchmen in any true interpretation of the term. We are the High Churchmen because with us the " ecclesia," the assembly of believers, is supreme. The Rector refers to the Salvation Army, and says that nobody ever speaks of till,: body as a "church." Perhaps not. The Salvation Army calls its meeting place a " barracks," to keep up the military terms that they have utilized. But if, some day, they should decide to adopt the more sacred title for their companies, and call them " churches," they have a perfect right to do so, and would be warranted by Scripture.

_ "OUTSIDE THE CHURCH." The Rector suggests that all Dissenters, the Army inclu- ded, are all on the Same level, and must be classed in the same category—" earnest bodies of people, work- ing "—outside the Church. Not so, Canon Willis. Out- side the Anglican Church, undoubtedly. But has the Anglican Episcopal Church any exclusive right to call itself the Church ? Is the Church of Jesus Christ confined to Anglican Episcopacy The clergy of the Roman Episcopal Church would not admit it for a moment. He excludes us, and all like us. They exclude him as well as all like us. We, on our part, exclude neither, but we do not mean to he excluded ourselves. I notice with con- siderable pleasure the kindly references which the Rector has made to myself, and am greatly touched by his remark that " God had recognized and blessed my ministry." Surely I can want nothing better than that. My regret is that while the Rector thus allows that God has given signs of recognition of my ministry his own recognition of it is so distant and partial. When the Rector spoke that kindly word he spoke as the man and the Christian, which is vastly better than his opinion as an Anglican ecclesiastic. When will the day come in which our brethren of the Episcopal and Estab- lished Church will come to see that Christian ministers whom God recognizes are worthy of recognition even by them? That day will come when the great principles for which Wycliffe contended 500 years ago win their destined triumph ; when men are guided by Scripture ; as the ultimate authority, and not by " the traditions of the eiders," when they are filled and pervaded by the SOrit of God, who is the Spirit of Liberty then "Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim." It is for that day that we shall never cease to pray and shall endeavour that no hard or bitter word of ours shall delay its coming. (Applause.) A vote of thanks was passed to Mr Yonge for his lecture, on the proposition of Mr WYLLIE, seconded by Mr G Buoys's, and supported by Mr W WALLINGTON, Mr POW/ORE and Mr GAULD.

A Warrington Captain's Death. Mr Brighouse conducted an inquiry at the Police Station on VVednesday evening respecting the death of John Gatley, of 10, Harboard-street, Warrington, employed as captain on board the flat " Ebro " belonging to the Manchester Ship Canal Company.l —The first witness called was Charles Gatley, son of the deceased, who stated that his father was 73 years of age. About one o'clock on Saturday after- noon he met his father in Scotland-road, he hav- ing just arrived by train from Manchester. Wit- ness noticed that his father looked ill an,l asked him what Was the matter. lie replied that he was on his boat in the dock at Manchester, and whilst walking along the deck he slipped and fell with hiel arms under him. On receiving his wages he decided to come home. Witness accompanied his father to the Infirmary, where he was detained as an in-patient. Witness saw him dead on the following 'lu,zsday. In answer to a question by the Coroner, witness said his father also told him that be got his arm hurt with some crates of earthenware at Liverpool. He did not say how it happened.—The Coroner said the doctor at the Infirmary reported that he found the deceased suffering from severe bruises on the shoulder and, wrist and he died from shock caused by the injuries. William Gatley,of 2 Bradshaw,street another son of the deceased said he saw his father at Liverpool on Thursday after the crates had been unladen and he did not complain of any injury. The foreman at the Manchester dock told witness that he took the deceased to the Salford Infirmary on Saturday morning. They examined the shoulder and said it was not broken.—Nuree Moore at the Warrington Infirmary stated that the deceased was admitted at 130 on Saturday. Dr Mort attended him. He died from shock to the system on the following Tues- day, The jury returned a verdict that the deceased died from shock caused by injuries, but there was An evidence to prove how he came by them.

div.head: RECTOR AND JOHN
div.p: THE RECTOR AND JOHN
WYCLIF FE.

Reply by the Rev. John Yonge. In connection with the Wycliffe Young People's Society, the Rev John Yonge delivered a lecture on Monday evening on "John Wycliffe." The lecture should have been delivered at the meeting of the society on the previous Monday liut Mr Yonge was unable to be present on that occasion. At the out- set, he said, one of the earliest sub3ects upon which he gave a lecture when first he came to Warring- ton was that upon which he desired to speak again that night. THE GREATEST OF ENGLISH PROTESTANT REFORMERS. It seemed then, and it seemed still,most desirable that they who belonged to a church bearing the name of Wycliffeshould know at least something about that great Christian Englishman and churchman. It might surprise some of them to realize that John Wycliffe was not a Congregationalist, and that he was not even a Noncon- formis%Theref were reasons to believe he would probably have been both if he had lived later than he did. But, as a matter of fact, he was as the Rector of Warrington claimed him the ;other day an English Churchman, and died while holding the Rectory of Lutterworth. They would see, however, in reviewing his history that he was the first and even the greatest of English Protest- ant reformers. It was of great importance to their young people especially that the great historic name that was often on their lips when referring to the church with which they were identified should be for them something very much more than a name. The name " W)cliffe " not only distinguished their church from St, Paul's, or St. Elphin's, or Trinity, from the Wesleyan or the Catholic or the Baptist Churches, the name stood for something, and it stood for a great deal. It even stood for every fundamental principle of Nonconformity and Congregationalism. Mr. J. D. Jones, of Bourne- mouth, told them the other day that their principles might be denoted as three—the open door, the open Bible, and the open mind. The open door—into the church and kingdom of Christ, through which any and all might enter who believed in Rico and acknowledged Him as Lord of all. Tne open Bible—as the book given by God not to a sect, not to a priesthood, not to a hier- archy, but to all men equal and alike, free to every reader, accessible to and acceptable by all who ' seek the light and truth of God. And the open mind— s mind, i.e. thankful to the past for all.it has handed down of understanding of Truth ravelled in the word of God, thankful to the present for all its increase of knowledge and wisdom concerning religion, and ready to receive from the futare whatever it might have to impart, believing as John Robinson, the Pilgrim Father said that the Lord loath yet more light and truth to bresk forth from His Word." All this the name of Wyc• liffe stood for, and therefore it stood for all that was fundamental in their Congregational faith and polity.
WYCLIFFE'S HOSTILITY TO HOME.

----- Reviewing the history of Wycliffe Mr yaw! said it was in the year 1360 that Wycliffe began his direct work as a controversialist and embarked in that enter- prise of hostility to Rome which thereafter made him so notorious, and had secured for him such a lasting im- mortality. He began a dispute with the Mendicant Friars and demanded not their reform, for that he deemed impossible, but thrir abolition. Against these Remish absolvers he declared war. It was a bold thing to do, but right was might with him and he left the issue. In the dispute which at this time arose between Enelanci and Rome about the annual tribute of 1,000 marks which King John had stipulated to pay, the opposition of the English Parliament to the demand of Rome was inspired from first to last by Wycliffe. He, 'it was, who was the first to assail and weaken the temporal power of the Pope in the land. His doctrines had by this time become widely I diffused, the clergy were alarmed at their spread and it waslconsidered necessary to "do something" to counteract his teaching. He was summoned to appear before Convocation on a charge of heresy, The lecturer described how the trial was stopped by the crowd, and Wycliffe returned home unmolested. He went on to refer to the Papal Bulls subsequently issued against him. to his later trial, the intervention of the Queen and his release. Wycliffe, he said, handed to his judges a paper containing a statement of his opinions with eanlanatiens of them. Among other opinions was this, that agitation in the direction of disendowment would be not only justifiable but necessary. He said "A state of things may arise,in which to deprive the Church of her wealth would be I much more Christian act than to have bestowed it upon her." Be (the lecturer) wondered whether churchmen of to—lay when they recalled these incidents of Wycliffe 's career would be all of them as ready to claim Wycliffe as "a devoted churchman, a strong churchman," as their friend the Rector was the other evening. There were some Anglicans, of course, who favoured disestablishment,but he did not remember to have heard of any who would agree to disendowment. His own belief was that the first involved the second and tbat one of these days the country would accom- plish both. He believed further that Wycliffe would have been favourable to tbe project, bad he lived to-day
THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY NOVEMBER 29, 1901

div.head: Coroner and the Railway Company.
div.p: The Coroner and the Railway Company.

The enquiry into the circumstances attending the death of a man who at the time was unknown, which took rlace at Earlestown Station on Thursday last, was held at the Town Hall,Eirlestown on Monday afternoon, by Mr 9 Brighouse coroner. Since the accident the man has been identified as James Belly a deaf mute.

Peter Jackson, lodging house keeper, Tontine-street, St. Helens, identified the deceased, who had been a " teaser " at Messrs Pilkington Bros. Glass Works, St. Helens. He had lodged with witness for about seven 'weeks, and appeared to be about 50 years of age, and was both deaf and dumb. Witness last saw him alive on the 18th November, he never saw him again until he was asked by a police officer to identify him on Friday. Andrew Rogers, a school boy, said that he met Kelly near Co Mr E T Evans' shop in Market-street, at 25 minutes to nine on Thursday mortOng. He showed witness a piece of paper which contained the words " direct this man to St. Helens side." Witness took him to the station, and they passed through the double doorway which was used for taking luggage on and off the station.

The Coroner: That is the door again. I knew what was coming. Witness continuing said both doors were open. The Coroner: Was there anyone there at the tirne ? Witness : Trucks were corning through 89 we went in. He further stated that when they got on the platform he took Kelly to the far side by way of the level crossing. The Coroner : D 1 you tell anyone about him. Witness : Yes, a porter. I told the porter he was deaf and dumb and wanted to go to St. Helens, I should know the porter if I saw him again, The Coroner: Where was he ?
Witness : He was on the other sids, on the middle platform against the steps, and I shouted to him across the line.

The Coroner: What did he say? Witness : He said, I must 890 another porter The man I spoke to worked in a cabin. A juror remarked that the witness spoken to was probably a signalman. Ia reply to the Coroner witness said that the trucks had got into the street when he and K:lly passed through the doors. The Coroner : Well I shall have something to say about these doors. We have talked about them before and I have told the Company over and over again about them. It had been said that this was only a simple ease. I don't think it is a simple case, we had a woman from Eccleston who found these doors wide open and walked through upon the level crossing and was killed. I have seen these doors open many times. Mr Carr, coroner's clerk, said the jury on that occa- sion recommended that the doors should be kept locked. The Coroner : I have seen the doors open on several I occasions, and no one near. I have drawn the atten- tion of the officials at Lime-street to the fact. People going in and out of the station ought to be under the direct supervision of the railway staff. Here was a case of a deaf and dumb man and a boy going on the station unnoticed. It was not the fault of the boy, but of the Company. To the witness: Was the man you spoke to a signal- manor a porter.

Witness said he was a signalman. He went up the Warrington line and into a cabin there. Mr Battersby (station master) said he had msde enquiries from the porters, but none of them admitted seeing the boy that morning. It might have been the signalmen at the Haydock crossing that the boy spoke to. , John Rearden, signalman at Haydock crossing was called.

The Coroner: Did you see this deaf and dumb man and the boy before the accident happened. Witness : No, sir ! The Coroner: What time did you go to the cabin ? Witness : Six o'clock. The Coroner repeated the boy's statement and asked witness if he could give them any idea who was on the station at the time. Witness said there would be no one except the porters The signalmen went on at six o'clock, two o'clock, and ten o'clock. He saw Kelly at the first crossing in the six-foot way, between the two four-feet. He was making his way to the down side. He appeared to be making slow progress crossing the line, and witness heard the engine whistle distinctly. Witness thought he was terribly slow. He was in a stooping position. It appeared to him looking from tho window of his cabin, that another .step would have saved him. He

_ was almost on the platform when he was struck by the engine. The result was he was thrown on the platform and killed. He ran to him but he was quite dead. The Coroner : Can you give the time. Witness : 9.28. The Coroner What I want to know is about these doors being open, and how it c.rrie about that tide man and lad went through without being observed. This was at 25 minutes to 9, 53 minutes had to be accounted for, and if the man was there ail the time, someone must have seen him. The Corones to Mr Battersby : Do you know any- thing about these doors. Mr Battersby : I know they were open at 8.35, to allow the greengrocers to go through. Mr Battersby was then sworn. Toe Coroner: You know there had been consider- able trouble about these doors.
Mr Battsr4by : I know you have complained about them.

The Coroner : T be quite straight and plain, you know you have had instructions from Lime-street about these doors in consequence of complaints I have made since the woman was killed on the station. I made those complaints in my capacity as a passenger. I complained to headquarters and they gave instruc- tions to you about these doors. Mr Battersby : Yes. _ _ _ _
The Coroner': What I say behind a man's back, I say to his race. What were the instructions about these doors ? Witness • To keep them closed when not in use.

Ths Coroner : When were these doors openel. Witness : At 8.35, to lot the greengrocers throu'lh. They were sometimes 10 minutes before they finished passing through. The Coroner ; Is there a porter to take charge of the doors ?
Witnefw : Not a specially appointed one. The Coroner •. What is there to prevent a passenger during that period from going on the line? Witne=s : Nothing whatever. _ . . . . . .

In reply to further questions the doors at the ticket office were inconvenient for perambulators and trucks on account of the steps. The Coroner : I don't want you to give the Company away but do you not think that arrangement could bs made that anyone going on or coming off the station would be under the observation of the man in the ticket office.

Witness thought it might be possible. The Coroner : It is a moderate idea and it is quit easy to do it. If that was done, anyone, before they got on your premises would have to pass a properly appointed person having a control of the station, and he would insist upon him going over the footbridge. We do not say anything about the accommodation for passeneers. The Foreman : There is none. The Coroner : Is it peasiole for any of these green- grocers to open the doors ? Witness : Not without the aid of the porters. The doors were fastened with a padlock, but it was possible to overlook the locking. The Coroner remarked that it was the worst appointed station on the line, and he would not care to be the station master. He was sorry for Mr Battersby having control of such a station, but he was not sorry for the Company. He knew Mr. Battorsby could not help it, it was his Company. The jury could see where the initial mistake had been made. They knew the station and its approaches. He did not know whether any of them were on the jury when that poor woman was killed. She and her sister went on the station because the doors were wide open. It was then said, and properly said. it was an invitation to the public to go through the doors. He, himself, would have thought the Company were inviting him to go that way, if the doors were wide open. The jury at that time made a strong pre- sentment about the doors. Now this accident had occurred. If there had been no doors, or if they had been closed, this deaf and dumb man would have bad to go to the other door, where ha would have been con- fronted by the ticket collector, and the boy wonld have told him that the man was deaf and dumb, and that he wanted to go to St Helene. They would have looked after the man then. A man with two infirmities was entitled to be looked after. Of course there was no legal obligation on the Company to do this, but there was a moral obligation. It was his opinion that the doors were open many times when they ought not to be. There was no blame to be attached to Mr. Battersby. He could not be everywhere. It was a large and un- wieldy station, a difficult station to manage. He could not be held responsible for this sort of thing, and no doubt did the best he could under the circumstances. It was a natural thing for the boy to take the ma through the doors when they were open. He said it quite courageously, as it was quite time the L. aad N.-W• Railway Company reorganised the station so as to make It impossible for persons to go on the station unless they passed throngh a place where someone was constanti y in attendance to direct them the right way. What the jury had to consider was whether this poor fellow dame by his death accidentally, and whether they could help to preserve life in the future by making some recom- mendation which he could send to the proper quarter. A juror said that from time to time it had been stated the Company intended to make some alteration. The Coroner : You know that the road to a certain place is paved with good intentions, (Laughter.) It was stated that the District Council had written about the station, and the question had been before them for two years. The Foreman : We are no nearer.
Mr Battersby said the plans were out. A Juror asked Mr BattEriby when alterations might be commenced.

Mr Battersby said he had no information. The Coroher said in any recommendation they had to make they must not be guided by what the Company proposed to do. The boy Rogers recalled said he saw the man on the platform about 6 minutes. The Coroner; You left the man in the hut, I mean the waiting room, for the Ist, 2ad and 3rd class passen- gers. Ido not like to say anything to hurt the feelings of the Company. Witness said be left the m'an there and crossed the line by the footbridge. The Coroner. It is curious you passed the ticket collector without having a ticket. Witness : There was no ticket collector. Mr Battereby explained there was a train due at the I curve at the time and the ticket collector was there. _ _

Robert Thomas Ratcliffe, post office clerk, said he saw the man struck by the expresJ as he was coming over the level crossing. The Coroner : Were these doors open 2 Witness : One of the doors was open. I was passing the station and was attracted by the shouts, and looked through the doorway. I did not notice anyone on the platform, nor a lorry outside the station. A verdict of Accidental death was returned, and the jury added a presentment that the existing doors used by passengers should be closed, a new booking office should be built nearer Queen-street, that a subway connecting each platform should be constructed and a person p'and in charge to prevent any person passing in or out except on business. They were of opinion that this accident had been brought about by the present un- satisfactory arrangements.

How the Firm came to be Formed. An Explanation in the Pulpit. Councillor F. R. Roberts was the preacher at the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday evening, in the place of Councillor Brough, who was indisposed. In the course of his remarks he said that after such a week as he had been spending, he would have been better sitting at home thinking things over, still when a man had got an easy conscience be need not be very much troubled about appeariag in a pulpit even after a week like that he had gone through. He could only say, so far as his part was concerned, there was nothing throughout the entire history of his connection with the firm inentioned (Ingrams Limited.) ef which he. was ashamed,or which if the thing was done. over again, he would not do again. The vrhole thing had been absolutely and entirely mie-represented, and he was sorry to say only one word could .133 applied to the case which had been b4ora the public, and that was a nasty little word, spelled in three letters. If they did not mind listening for a few moments be would tell I them in a few words his action in the car, as he felt he I himself in appearing in a Constian pulpit. mAufeswt justify vhs Fog) a young fellow came to him and told him he was doing a nice business as an electrician' He was sadly hampered by the need of funds, because of the very expensive stock required in such a trade, and he needed a good deal more money than he had. He put the fittinin in his (the speaker's) own office so ex- cellently well that he was very much impressed with him, and made further inquiries about him. He found that the young fellow bad been the entire support of his family,and that his father had been blind for nine years All that time he had supported them. He thought they would agree that if there was one thing in connection with that young men to his credit it was that, and every opportunity should be taken to help such a rising young man. When he discovered that, a few friends and himself decided to subscribe £5O each and set him in business. They did not wish to run any more risk, and theretore they re- gistered it as a company with limited liability. The , young fel!ow had been very successful, and they left everything, and desired to leave everything, to his own discretion. He applied for the Corporation contract to put fittings in the new police buildings, but that was altogether out of their knowledge. Tnat simple act of brotherly friendliness—for which they had not yet re- ceived a single sixponce in return—bad been twisted and warped into what they had heard last week, and his (the speaker's) name had been dragged through the mud in a way it was never dragged before. They had challenged their slanderers fir what had been said against them and, miek his word, that challenge wonll never be accepted. He had remarked that they did not know that the con- tract was applied for, but supposing he had known, when the company was formed, that it was the inten- tion to apply to get corporation work, what was wrong in that so long as they were doing work for the Corpora- tion in the cheapest and best possible way ? What was wrong, he asked again i) He asked them to believe himl to be as absolutely free from complicity in any wrong doing as the youngest child in the chapel that night. Bat, mark his words, they would be able tc give the lie in the teeth of the slanderers to what they had said. He then proceeded to give a temperance address—it being temperance Sunday—during which he said that all teetotalers were not charitable. The man NOBTBIWICH-18, APPLEMARKET-STRE ET from Manchester on Thursday was a teetotaler and also a member of the United Kingdom Alliance, but he FRIDAY, 11 to 12, and 1 to h. was wanting in the saving grace of charity. If the whole of the Roberts family had not been teetotalers there would not have been the hubbub there had been of late in the town. It was because a large number did not like them because they were teetotalers, that so much had been said against them. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A HAT'DOCN COLLIER. Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held the inquest on Monday evening at the Waggon Hotel, Haydock, on William Turner, aged 40, of Haydock, who died in the Cottage Hospital on Saturday morning from injuries received the previous day at the Southport pit, Parr. The Coroner read a letter from Mr Hall, Government Inspector, who said that deceased and another man were lowering a tub full of refuse down a steep incline, and it caught the side and stuck. Deceased went in front and tried to loosen it, though he was warned by his mate to keep at the high side. When the tub got loose it over- powered the men and carried deceased down the brow. The deceased's action was foolish and a breach of special rule 51, which said that every- body must keep behind the box.—James Hasleden, of 330, Park-road, Sc. Helens, said he and deceased filled the box. When deceased went in front of the box and loosened it it dashed away, carrying him twenty or twenty-five yards. They picked him up with a broken leg and shoulder injured.— The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," "

SANKEY ALBION V. BARLEBTOWN AMATEURS. Played at Sankey on Saturday, no goals being se-med. WARRINGTON " GUARDIAN " V. BEWSEY ALL SAINTS. Played at Arpley on Saturday. Result ;—Saints, two goals; " Guardian," nil. WARRINGTON ST. AUSTIN'S V, BURTONWOOD. Played at Warrington. The visitors had the best of the opening exchanges, several fine shots being stopped by Glover and Blackshaw. From a corner Laylor registered the first goal for Burtonwood. The visitors tried hard to equalise, but failed. Half-time :—Burtonwood, one goal ; St. Austin's, nil. During the second half the aints struggled hard to gain an equalizing goal, but the defence Jf Burton wood proved sound, and they won by one goal to nil.

JOHNSON, 43, plaintiff and the defendant was represented by Mr HOLFORD-WARE, LONDON W.O Glover, of Smetlawick. Plaintiff's case was that she was engaged by the defendant to take a leading part in " A life's revenge" and had to purchase very expensive dresses. Miss Dagmar advanced her £5 towards the cost of the dresses and plaintiff admitted owing that amount. In one scene she had to fight a duel with Miss Dagmar. The play was presented at Warrington in October and on the second night plaintiff sustained an injury in the duel scene. She, however, continued to play until Friday night when, having seen Ds Peacock, she was obliged to take to her bed and had been medically attended ever since. When the Company left Warrington plaintiff received a letter from defendant stating that she could not pos- sibly take her to Birmingham, where tne play was to be presented the next week. It seemed impossible, she said, for plaintiff to fight the duel. Subsequently plain- tiff received a letter from defendant's manager to the effect that her dresses would be taken on loan until she had repaid the £5 which she owed defendant. The dresses would be worn by the lady who succeeded her in the part. The dresses had been retained until the present time, and plaintiff objected to wearing them after tney had been worn by another actress. It was contended that defendant was not justified in retaining the dresses until the debt was discharged, view which his Honour upheld. For the defence it was stated that the dreses were not worth more than £6. Defendant and several witnesses, including Mr Joseph Potter, manager of the Royal Court Theatre, gave evidence to this effect. His Honour gave judgment for the return of the dresses, &ic, or in the alternative payment of £2l 3.; id, which he estimated as their value, with £3 damages for wrongful detention, and costs.
